pistons.headline: Pistons vs Magic final score: Detroit’s dominant defense shows up with Cade Cunningham sidelined
pistons.body:
ORLANDO, FLORIDA - NOVEMBER 24: Isaiah Joe #17 of the Detroit Pistons reacts after scoring a three-pointer against the Orlando Magic during the fourth quarter of a Emirates NBA Cup game at Kia Center on November 24, 2026 in Orlando, Florida. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Rich Storry/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The Goin to Work Pistons showed up tonight. Detroit dispatched the Orlando Magic 104-86. This was another statement game. It doesn’t matter who plays; defense travels. Detroit is now 2-1 in NBA Cup play with a plus-31 point differential. Orlando felt Detroit’s defensive wrath, holding Orlando to 14 second-quarter points. They were everywhere.

Cade Cunningham was a late scratch, but the next man steps up here. Both teams struggled to put the ball in the hoop, but Detroit generated better shots. They swung the ball from side to side on plenty of possessions. The shot-making results weren’t always there, but their process was solid. It was probably more than solid considering they were down three starters tonight.

Ausar Thompson and Daniss Jenkins picked up more on-ball reps. Jenkins had a 15-point and 10-assist double-double. Thompson continues to grow as a playmaker for others as he added seven more assists tonight.

Ausar seems much more sure of himself this season. Even the moments he turns down shots to find a teammate are telling — everything seems planned.

Ausar wasn’t the only Piston with an all-around A performance. Kevin Huerter finished with 13-5-6. He worked the off-ball screen here, slightly froze the big, and threw an accurate lob to Paul Reed.

The OOP 🎯 pic.twitter.com/VetSoIuf8f
— Detroit Pistons (@DetroitPistons) November 25, 2026

Isaiah Joe led the team with 21 points. He went 5-for-11 from trey. Joe showed off the range and confidence. He pressured the ball on the other end. Shooters competing on defense, and not being must-hide defenders, is such a plus. Joe is picking it up.

Ron Holland has success from deep. He buried two 3s. Detroit shot it well as a team despite their low point total. They went 15-for-36 from deep compared to Orlando’s 12-for-36. John Collins, Woo, and Elijah Harkless (he made some momentum-swinging ones) all hit two 3s.

Detroit knocked down 3s but kept Orlando from doing anything. Franz Wagner had been on a hot streak until he ran into this defense (29 PPG over the last 10). He (20 pts) and Desmond Bane (21 pts) put numbers on the board, but it wasn’t easy. Those two saw a crowd every time they drove the ball. Wagner started spamming push shots that felt automatic, but Detroit held him in check.

Anthony Black was a non-factor offensively tonight. That’s a testament to Detroit’s D, as he’s been rolling all year. The Magic missed so many shots at the rim. They were initially dominating Detroit on the offensive glass, but those missed shots eventually turned into Detroit run-outs.

The Pistons also got their hands on so many Magic passes tonight. They made Orlando creators play with multiple hands in their faces and trusted their closeouts to disrupt “open” Orlando 3s. Holding a team under 90 in 2026 is some Goin to Work stuff. Hats off to J.B. Bickerstaff for having this defense ready to go at all times.

Detroit’s final group play cup game is Friday versus the flaming hot Tyler Herro and the Milwaukee Bucks. Detroit could still win the group even after losing to the Toronto Raptors last Friday. They might need some help, but must start by handling their business with the Bucks.

Jalen Duren remains out as he works his way back from a hamstring strain. That’s unfortunate because I am desperate to see what this team looks like with Duren back in the fold and eager to leave behind the John Collins starting-center era for good. In Detroit’s most recent loss against the Atlanta Hawks, they were outrebounded by 19 and outscored in the paint 27-6. Tonight, they face the Orlando Magic. Orlando has righted the ship a bit, winning five of its past seven games. They win by protecting the paint, and that has been Detroit’s Achilles’ heel since Duren went down. They don’t let you score inside, and their defense is top 5 in limiting second-chance points, paint points, and fast-break points. Detroit is not going to find a clear path to easy points, which means their half-court offensive execution must improve significantly over their recent outings.

pistons.headline: Pistons at Hawks final score: Detroit outscored by 21 in the fourth, lose 107-97
pistons.body:
ATLANTA, GEORGIA - NOVEMBER 22: Nickeil Alexander-Walker #7 of the Atlanta Hawks reacts after hitting a three-point basket against the Detroit Pistons during the first quarter at State Farm Arena on November 22, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images) | Getty Images

That was an unbelievable collapse by Detroit, and quite possibly the worst game of Cade Cunningham’s career.

The Pistons went into the fourth quarter with an 85-74 lead. They outscored the Hawks by 10 in the third quarter, and ESPN had Detroit at a 90% chance to win the game when the final frame started.

That went downhill quickly as the Hawks went on an 18-0 run to open the fourth quarter. The Pistons didn’t score their first points until Isaiah Joe hit a corner three with 4:52 left in the game. Detroit’s offense stalled, the ball wasn’t moving, and for whatever reason, Cade Cunningham and Daniss Jenkins took it upon themselves to try to iso Dyson Daniels and Lu Dort. As you can tell, it didn’t work.

Detroit shot better from the field, the three-point line, and the free-throw line. They even scored more points in the paint than the Hawks, but couldn’t manage to grab a rebound. Atlanta grabbed 19 more rebounds than Detroit and outrebounded the Pistons on the offensive glass 24-8. If there was ever a game that showed Detroit needed Jalen Duren back ASAP, this was it.

Atlanta had 10 more fastbreak points than Detroit, and second-chance points went in a massive favor of the Hawks to the tune of 27-6. Detroit’s rebounding was horrendous – outside of Ausar Thompson’s 11 boards, John Collins was second on the team with six.

Cade Cunningham scored in single digits for the first time all season with five points while shooting 2-for-9 from the field. He also added four rebounds and 15 assists in what is surely one of the weirdest stat lines of his career. Kevin Huerter was a -28 on the floor while shooting 1-for-8 for a measly two points.

Oddly enough, it was Isaiah Joe who led the team in scoring with 19 points on 15 attempts. Joe was +11 tonight and knocked down three threes. John Collins and Ausar Thompson each had 18 points. Collins made four threes, and Ausar added five assists. Paul Reed had 16 points off the bench, and Daniss Jenkins had 11.

In what should’ve been a victory tonight in Atlanta, Detroit blew their double-digit lead and deserved to lose this game. That was one of the worst fourth quarter performances I’ve ever watched, and it looked like a middle school team that couldn’t grab a rebound in a scrimmage against the high school varsity.

Please, Jalen Duren, come back soon.

Detroit moves to 10-6 on the year and will now travel to Orlando to take on the Magic on Tuesday night. Let’s hope this Pistons team has a short memory and burns tonight’s fourth quarter tape.

Go Stones.

pistons.headline: Pistons vs. Raptors final score: Cade vs. Scottie battle goes to Raps
pistons.body:
[DETROIT, MI - NOVEMBER 20: Cade Cunningham #2 of the Detroit Pistons plays defense on Scottie Barnes #4 of the Toronto Raptors during the 2026 Emirates NBA Cup on November 20, 2026 at Little Caesars Arena in Detroit, Michigan. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Chris Schwegler/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

Two former teammates and two Eastern Conference teams traded body blows all night. A Cade Cunningham 3-pointer to put the Pistons up 102-101 with 20 seconds left was answered by a Scottie Barnes driving layup over two defenders to give the Raptors the lead they would not relinquish. When a Kevin Huerter three came up short as the buzzer sounded, it was decided. Raptors 105-102.

Cunningham led Detroit with 23 points and nine assists, but he was outshined on this night by his former Montverde teammate Barnes, who led all scorers with 29 points and hit his first nine shots of the night.

While it was appointment television watching the two top players on each team matched up with each other, the rest of the game was pretty much a horror show for the Pistons. Distilling why the Pistons dropped this game will sound very familiar to Pistons fans — not owning the paint.

Detroit surrendered 54 points inside to Toronto and gave up crucial offensive rebounds late. It’s one thing to see Barnes put a great game on you, but Detroit was owned inside by rookie Allen Graves making his first start of the season. He scored 20 points, had 10 rebounds, including four on the offensive end. Detroit simply had no answer for him. Certainly not John Collins.

The overmatched emergency starting center struggled again in just under 20 minutes of action. He was just 1-of-4 from the floor for three points and six rebounds. The return of Isaiah Joe from injury isn’t looking very different from when he was playing early in the season — he’s still struggling to find his shot. Joe was 1-of-6 from deep tonight. Getting those kinds of performances from your two highest-profile offseason acquisitions is not the recipe for winning basketball.

The other major issue tonight is that you were facing one of the worst-shooting offenses in the NBA and on this night, they could not miss. Some of that had to do with Detroit’s occasionally passive defense. But tonight, the Raptors players were just collectively on one. We already covered how hot Barnes was, especially early, but the sweet shooting was up and down the roster.

The rookie Graves was 6-of-9, Jakob Poeltl was 5-of-7, and Immanuel Quickly was 6-of-10. Collectively, Toronto shot 67% inside the arc tonight. Again, I’m going to point to the big black hole in the middle of Detroit’s lineup. A combination of John Collins and Paul Reed as your only big men is just not going to get it done in the NBA. The Pistons need Jalen Duren to come back desperately.

The loss to the Raptors drops the Pistons to 1-1 in NBA Cup play, but then again, I refuse to care about the NBA Cup. Detroit now goes on a mini road trip to Atlanta on Sunday and Orlando on Tuesday before enjoying seven of the next eight games at home.

The Toronto Raptors are scuffling in the first leg of the NBA season, but there is certainly a lot of talent there. Yes, Kawhi Leonard is absent with news of managing knee pain and swelling that surely puts a shiver up the spine of every Toronto fan. But they also still have Scottie Barnes, and he is delivering the young star goods as advertised. He is averaging 23.8 points, 7.4 rebounds, and 4.7 assists a night. On certain nights, he looks like the young superstar that represents his clearly attainable ceiling. On other nights, he and his team’s offense struggle and can’t seem to get unstuck from the mud. He’s doing a lot of things, but he isn’t doing it as efficiently or consistently as you’d like.

The real problems with the Raptors, though, lie elsewhere. Nobody can seemingly hit a three. RJ Barrett is getting to the line five times a game and hitting just 60% from the charity stripe. Collin Murray-Boyles has regressed, and Jakob Poeltl’s game has fallen off a cliff. It feels like if you solve Scottie, it helps you solve Barrett and Immanuel Quickley, and therefore, you solve the Raptors. Toronto has dropped six straight, and will be without the services of Barrett tonight.

Watching an Ausar Thompson and Scottie Barnes matchup could be electric. Barnes doesn’t have the defensive chops Ausar does, and Ausar doesn’t have the offensive versatility, but both could be liable to pull off a triple-double tonight. Cade Cunningham is also expected back tonight after sitting out Detroit’s win against the New Orleans Pelicans. Duncan Robinson and Ron Holland are out, and doubtful, respectively.

pistons.body:
DETROIT, MI - OCTOBER 16: Isaiah Joe #17 of the Detroit Pistons shoots the ball during the game against the Toronto Raptors on October 16, 2026 at Little Caesars Arena in Detroit, Michigan. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Brian Sevald/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

Early season Fridays = NBA Cup day! The Detroit Pistons can climb to 2-0 in group play with a win over the worse-than-expected Toronto Raptors (1-1 in group play). The NBA thought this would’ve been a big game, handing out the Prime Video first game slot, but injuries, injuries, injuries.

Ron Holland, Duncan Robinson, and Jalen Duren are out again, but Cade Cunningham is expected to play. Injuries have slowed down the Raptors a ton.

RJ Barrett and Collin Murray-Boyles won’t suit up in Detroit. Kawhi Leonard remains out. His absence is the main source of Toronto’s struggle, but I still expected more.

GAME VITALS

Where: Little Caesars Arena, Detroit, MI

When: 7:30 PM ET

Watch: Prime Video

Odds: Pistons (-6.5)

The Raptors are still live even though they should be better. That said, Detroit isn’t a team that takes opponents lightly because of who’s in or out. The Pistons play the same brand of ball regardless of who’s out there on either side.

Wednesday’s 122-109 win over the New Orleans Pelicans tripled down on that point. Even a shorthanded Pistons squad without Cade manages to find a way.

Daniss Jenkins. Javonte Green. Ausar Thompson with the ball. Paul Reed with extended minutes — trustworthy things.

We got Isaiah Joe back in the lineup in that one! One of the marquee signings of Detroit’s offseason let it fly. Joe went 3-for-5 from range and put it on the floor, aiding Detroit’s flow. Bball Paul said Joe had more in his game during media day. Paul knows ball.

What do you know, it's Isaiah Joe

-Pistons able to flow into early offense with nothing there on initial push. DHO and now Joe gets a flare with an empty side
-Huerter cuts backdoor, pindown for Joe with an empty side. Turns the corner and the lob is there. pic.twitter.com/LZ8FQlRRAH
— Steve Jones (@stevejones20) November 19, 2026

The ability to leverage your shooting with live dribble decisions is an invaluable skill come playoff time. Love seeing Joe back out there, and more of that would be cool.

John Collins was on a heater (4-6 on 3s). He should get six 3s up every night with the room he has to fire. Collins will be matched up with Jakob Poeltl tonight. Poeltl is arguably the biggest hacker in the league. His 5.6 foul percentage ranks in the fourth percentile among bigs.

A lot of those Cade drives should end with trips to the charity stripe. Cade’s .37 FTr is a career high. He’s getting the calls and shooting ~86 percent at the line. That works. Cade is also putting together a strong All-Defense case, being a big-time contributor on the sixth-best defense.

Per Stathead, only Cade, Nikola Jokić, Matisse Thybulle, Scottie Barnes, and Caleb Wilson are averaging at least 0.9 blocks and 1.4 steals. Cade is doing this without fouling. He’s leveling up even more on that end.

Barnes recently declared himself the best defender in the world. I have no problem with that. He is up there. He’s a legit 1-5 defender. Anybody that good at something should feel they’re the best. That confidence got them where they are.

Barnes is Barnes, but I thought Toronto would have a more intimidating team defense. Cleaning The Glass ranks them 17th overall and 19th over the past two weeks + they are on a six-game losing streak.

The injury bug cannot be ignored, but I thought Toronto would be immune to long stretches of defensive lapses because of their suffocating gap principles.

Those principles still force turnovers at a frightening rate (2nd), but they haven’t dug in and clamped down like last year’s Raptors team. They’re still feisty enough to muddy up a game, but I expected more.

Toronto’s off-the-bounce creation takes a big blow with no Kawhi and Barrett. Barnes has more shot-making responsibilities this season. His 23.8 points per game are a career high. Immanuel Quickley will get them up. Catching fire vs. Ausar and the Pistons’ defense isn’t easy, but Toronto is looking to Quickley to provide immediate offense.

Jamison Battle is one of Toronto’s consistent snipers. He’s not a shooter you can disregard and is coming off a 19-point, 5-for-10 from 3 game. Ja’Kobe Walter can shoot it too and is quietly turning into a dependable heavy-minute wing.

With a win, Detroit could be in first or second in the East Group A division. The Orlando Magic (2-0) take on the struggling Brooklyn Nets (0-1) tonight. Should Orlando snag a win, they stay atop the group.

One game and one week at a time for Detroit in this tournament. They smacked around the Nets in their first cup game and look to do the same against the Raptors.

Projected starting lineup

Detroit Pistons (10-4): Cade Cunningham, Daniss Jenkins, Kevin Huerter, Ausar Thompson, John Collins

Toronto Raptors (5-10): Immanuel Quickley, Ja’Kobe Walter, Jamison Battle, Scottie Barnes, Jakob Poeltl

Question of the Day

The New York Knicks won the NBA Cup tourney and the real thing last year. Did that add any validity to the tournament?

pistons.headline: Pistons at Pelicans final score: No Cade, No Problem
pistons.body:
NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - NOVEMBER 18: Paul Reed #7 of the Detroit Pistons dunks in front of Karlo Matković #17 of the New Orleans Pelicans during the first half of a game at Smoothie King Center on November 18, 2026 in New Orleans, Louisiana. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Tyler Kaufman/Getty Images) | Getty Images

With as long as Detroit’s injury report has been recently, it got a little longer with Cade Cunningham as a late addition tonight. After the Pistons’ big win against San Antonio last night, it’s no surprise Deuce got some rest on the second night of a back-to-back.

JB Bickerstaff, with his shorthanded roster, rolled out the unusual starting lineup of Daniss Jenkins, Kevin Huerter, Javonte Green, Ausar Thompson, and John Collins. This would’ve been a great game for Ebuka Okorie to get some minutes, but he hurt his hip with the Motor City Cruise just the other day.

This meant Detroit’s key bench pieces were Paul Reed, Chaz Lanier, and Elijah Harkless. Even Tolu Smith saw some spot minutes when Collins and Reed both needed rest. Luckily, Isaiah Joe made his return to the lineup tonight after missing the last several games. Despite having to play guys from the end of the bench and on two-way spots, Detroit didn’t struggle against New Orleans.

Remember that unusual starting lineup for Detroit? Well, every single one of them finished in double digits. Jenkins, Green, and Collins all made at least three three-pointers. Jenkins, Thompson, and Huerter all had at least four assists, though Huerter had seven and DJ added nine.

Both Lanier and Joe made three three-pointers off the bench. Reed was the key sixth man once again, though that’s not all that peculiar nowadays. Harkless played his most minutes so far this season and did a great job sharing the rock with four assists.

In a game without their star player, this was another complete team win. There’s no doubt the depth on this team is one of the best in the league, and Detroit had seven different players score in double digits. Your Detroit Pistons are now 10-4 on the year.

Be sure you didn’t miss the lob finish by Woo:

— Detroit Pistons (@DetroitPistons) November 19, 2026

In an ultimate bit of disrespect, the Detroit Pistons are resting star Cade Cunningham tonight against the New Orleans Pelicans. The reasoning appears to be twofold — 1. Cunningham played last night. 2. The Pelicans. The poor, beleaguered Pelicans, home to former Pistons executives Joe Dumars and Troy Weaver, are not having a smooth go of it early in the season. They are 5-10, the coach is fighting with players, and a starter has already asked for a trade. That doesn’t mean there isn’t talent on the team. lions.headline: Former Detroit Lions owner Martha Firestone Ford dies at age 101
lions.body:
DETROIT, MI - NOVEMBER 24: Detroit Lions Head Coach Dan Campbell talks with Detroit Lions Owner/Chair Emeritus Martha Firestone Ford during pregame prior to the Detroit Lions versus the Green Bay Packers game on Sunday November 6, 2022 at Ford Field in Detroit, MI. (Photo by Steven King/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images

The Detroit Lions announced on Tuesday night that former team owner Martha Firestone Ford has passed away at age 101. According to the team, she passed away at her home surrounded by family.

Ford took over as principal owner of the franchise in 2014, following the death of her husband, William Clay Ford. She held onto the role until 2020, when she bequeathed primary ownership to her daughter and current Lions owner Sheila Hamp.

Since then, Ford has been serving as Owner/Chair Emeritus of the team. Here’s how the team described her role over the past six years.

In her most recent role as Owner/Chair Emeritus, Mrs. Ford supported her four children – Principal Owner/Chair Sheila Ford Hamp, Owner/Vice Chair Martha Ford Morse, Owner/Vice Chair William Clay Ford Jr., and Owner/Vice Chair Elizabeth Ford Kontulis – as they assumed leadership responsibilities within the family franchise. Today the Ford family proudly carries forward the legacy established by Mr. and Mrs. Ford, preserving the values, love, and passion that have shaped a family tradition spanning multiple generations.

During Mrs. Ford’s brief stint as primary owner, the Lions made the playoffs twice (2014, 2016) and produced three winning seasons.

The team offered this official statement on Ford’s passing:

“It is with heavy hearts that we acknowledge the passing of Martha Firestone Ford. Mrs. Ford inspired us all as a pillar of the Detroit community and the passionate matriarch of the Detroit Lions football team.

“She will always be remembered for her fierce loyalty to her family, her community, and the city of Detroit.

“Her presence on our sideline, in our building, and in our community will be greatly missed. We wish the entire Ford and Firestone families peace in this time of mourning.”

For more on Mrs. Ford’s passing and her life accomplishments, check out the Detroit Lions’ official story.

The Detroit Lions (8-2) and Chicago Bears (8-2) will square off in this year’s Thanksgiving Day battle, and for the second straight day, the Lions and Bears have opted for walkthrough practices.

A walkthrough practice means that all participation levels are estimates from the coaching staff based on how the player would have participated in a traditional practice. So, with that in mind, let’s look at Tuesday’s injury report and get you up to date on what we know.

Note: Any changes from the most recent injury report will be bolded

Estimated no practice

DT Skyler Gill-Howard (knee) — Update: His season is over

EDGE DJ Wonnum (back)

CB Ennis Rakestraw (shoulder)

Gill-Howard’s knee injury is significant enough to require surgery and will end his rookie season. A staple of the Lions’ three-man interior defensive line, the Lions will need more production from their depth players beyond starters Alim McNeill and Tyleik Williams.

“Sky is out for the year. He has a knee injury that will require surgery, so he’ll be out. I hate that for him. He’s had a heck of a season up until this point,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said on Tuesday. Later adding, “He’s done a really good job for us. But we’ve still got Mac (McNeill), we still have Tyleik, we’ve still got Levi (Onwuzurike), we’ve got (Tyler) Lacy that can play in there. Could see (Mekhi) Wingo. Wonnum played a full allotment of snaps last Sunday, but his injury appeared to pop up afterward and is significant enough to make him a game-time decision on Thursday, per Campbell. New injuries can be brutal on a short week, but there’s still room for optimism.

Rakestraw’s injury kept him out of last weekend’s game, so starting the week with continued restrictions isn’t a great sign for his availability. Campbell didn’t say it directly, but he’ll likely be a game-time decision, too.

Estimated limited practice

lions.headline: Detroit Lions lose another defender to season-ending injury
lions.body:
DETROIT,MICHIGAN-NOVEMBER 22: Defensive tackle Skyler Gill-Howard (50) of the Detroit Lions looks on from the sidelines during an NFL football game between the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and the Detroit Lions in Detroit, Michigan USA, on Sunday, November 22, 2026. (Photo by Amy Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images

The injuries to the Detroit Lions defense are starting to mount. On Tuesday, Lions coach Dan Campbell revealed that rookie defensive tackle Skyler Gill-Howard is out for the rest of the season with a knee injury sustained during the team’s win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Sunday. Campbell said the injury occurred when Gill-Howard was in the game during a goal-line play on offense.

“Sky is out for the year. He’s out for the year. He had a knee injury that will require surgery. So he’ll be out,” Campbell said. “I hate that for him. He’s had a heck of a season up to this point.”

It’s the third significant injury to a Lions defender in the past four weeks, joining linebacker Jack Campbell (neck) and Aidan Hutchinson (torn ACL).

Gill-Howard, the team’s sixth-round pick this year, was one of the most pleasant surprises from Detroit’s defense this year. He’s played 316 defensive snaps through 10 games, tallying 2.0 sacks, six quarterback hits, and a tackle for loss.

His loss, combined with Hutchinson’s season-ending injury, leaves the Lions a bit shorthanded on the defensive line in terms of pass rushers, but Campbell said it is an opportunity for several players to step up in his absence.

“We still got Mac (Alim McNeill), we’ve got Tyleik (Williams), we’ve got Levi (Onwuzurike), we’ve got (Tyler) Lacy who can play in there. It could be (Mekhi) Wingo. Could be Taki (Taimani), could be AK (Aidan Keanaaina). So we’ve got options there,” Campbell said. “But you hate to lose a player like him. He’s had a heck of a rookie season. We’ve mentioned this, but for a young guy, he’s a pro. He’s conscientious in what he did, just the right approach.”

lions.headline: NFL Week 12 power rankings: Lions a consensus Top 10 team for first time this season
lions.body:
Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell cheers on against Tampa Bay Buccaneers during the second half at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

The Detroit Lions (8-2) are riding a six-game win streak and coming off another strong performance, beating the Tampa Bay Buccaneers 31-21 in a game that wasn’t as close as the score suggests.

The Lions land in the Top 10 in every national power ranking for the first time this season, and while most analysts are enamored with the offense—specifically superstar Jahmyr Gibbs—many still can’t get past their lack of confidence in the defense. The Lions will have a chance to change that narrative this week when they host the Chicago Bears on Thanksgiving—note: all but one ranker has the Bears ahead of the Lions, save NFL.com—but for now, they’ll remain the underdog.

Let’s take a closer look at this week’s national power rankings.

NFL.com: 5 (Previous rank: 8)

From Nick Shook:

Detroit has quietly become one of the most consistent and comfortably predictable teams in the NFL over the last two months, reliably producing offense in a fashion that is thankfully becoming less dependent on Jahmyr Gibbs, while coupling it with a defense that is steadily improving despite new injury losses. The Lions are not as flashy as the 49ers or Bears, nor are they as intimidating as Minnesota’s defense (save for Week 11), but they’re a well-rounded, winning football team that clearly isn’t going away anytime soon. Sunday’s win over the Buccaneers was just another example of this.

CBS Sports: 6 (Previous rank: 8)

From Pete Prisco:

The improvement of the defense is a good sign. They might not have Aidan Hutchinson or Jack Campbell, but they are playing much better on that side of the ball.

Sporting News: 6 (Previous rank: 8)

From Vinnie Iyer:

Jahmyr Gibbs deserves some more MVP discussion. He leads the NFL with 267 touches, 1,098 rushing yards, 1,502 scrimmage yards and 15 total TDs after scoring two more against the Buccaneers. He’s on pace for 2,550 scrimmage yards and 26 TDs, which would be one of the best running back seasons ever.

The Athletic: 6 (Previous rank: 9)

From Chad Graff and Josh Kendall:

Something to be thankful for: Ford Field

Only the Bills have won more home games since 2023 than the Lions, who improved to 5-0 at Ford Field on Sunday. They are 26-8 at home since the start of Dan Campbell’s third season. The site of Detroit’s annual Thanksgiving game, where it will be Thursday against the Bears, hasn’t always been so friendly to the home team. From 2000 to 2022, the Lions had the second-lowest home winning percentage in the league (.427).

ESPN: 6 (Previous rank: 10)

From ESPN Staff, excerpt from Eric Woodyard:

Extension candidate: S Brian Branch

Branch and TE Sam LaPorta are playing out the 2026 season on their four-year rookie deals, but general manager Brad Holmes has reiterated that he would like to reach long-term extensions with both players, though LaPorta has expressed doubts. Branch has made an immediate impact since returning from an Achilles injury that he sustained in Week 7 of last season. In 2026, he has five passes defended and one interception in four games. Depending on how the rest of the season plays out for Branch, the Lions could use the franchise tag or agree to long-term deal with him.

USA Today: 7 (Previous rank: 10)

From Nate Davis:

RB Jahmyr Gibbs will rightly continue to command quite a bit of the spotlight as he keeps trending toward 2,500 yards from scrimmage and potentially breaking Chris Johnson’s single-season record (2,509). But how about a hand for a decimated defense that’s held up pretty well so far without injured stars Aidan Hutchinson and Jack Campbell?

Yahoo Sports: 8 (Previous rank: 11)

From Frank Schwab:

Detroit’s first defensive test without Aidan Hutchinson went well. The Lions allowed just 274 yards and 21 points, and Tampa Bay got 65 yards and a touchdown on a meaningless drive at the end of a game when Detroit led by 17 points. The Lions had four sacks, which was a good sign. The Lions’ defense has been much better since the first few weeks of the season, and Sunday’s game was without Hutchinson and linebacker Jack Campbell.

The test Thursday will be tougher, with the Chicago Bears coming in with first place in the NFC North on the line. But if Detroit’s defense can maintain this level, the Lions might be a Super Bowl contender. That could reveal itself on Thanksgiving.

“Our guys are competitive, man, and they don’t want to be counted out,” Lions head coach Dan Campbell said of the defense’s performance Sunday, via the team’s site. “And nobody cares. There are no excuses. And the only way to gain respect is just go about your business, man, and make plays and play together and prove your worth, man.”

Sports Illustrated: 10 (Previous rank: 9)

From Connor Orr:

Dan Campbell has been proven right to this point on Kelvin Sheppard. He stuck by his defensive coordinator, and now his defensive coordinator may see more head coaching interview opportunities based on how well he’s handled all of the adversity foisted onto the Lions’ defense. From Terrion Arnold to Jack Campbell to Aidan Hutchinson…it’s been a long season.

lions.headline: Film study: Jahmyr Gibbs in motion creates space for teammates
lions.body:
Detroit Lions offensive coordinator Drew Petzing watches a play against Tampa Bay Buccaneers during the first half at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

All Grit. The Detroit Lions won their 6th straight game, knocking off the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, maintaining the top spot in the NFC North. Let’s take a look at those standings.

Breathe it in. It feels good. It feels like everything is exactly as it should be.

Ben Johnson makes his second return to Ford Field this Thanksgiving, leading the Chicago Bears into town boasting their own 8-2 record. They’re the darlings. The genius head coach. The dynamic quarterback. Every talking head’s favorite team to win the NFC.

Good.

As our own Ryan Matthews pointed out, Jared Goff looks and acts just as good as the real thing—the MVP quarterbacks who garner all of the attention—but his name isn’t Joe or Josh. That same misfit-toys metaphor applies to Lions offensive coordinator Drew Petzing compared to Johnson. Sure, he might be a little shorter in stature and has been given the nickname “Megamind,” but Petzing’s offense looks and plays just as well as Ben the boy wonder’s.

And if Petzing keeps getting overlooked nationally, the Lions could be fortunate enough to keep their offensive coordinator for the foreseeable future. If the stigma of his three-year stint as the playcaller in Arizona stays with him, good. Detroit will gladly retain him.

For this film study, I want to put one play design element under the microscope: presnap motion. Not just any presnap motion, but utilizing the NFL’s best offensive weapon to create space.

Stretching the seams

Todd Bowles and the Buccaneers’ defensive unit have a history of being stout, resulting in frustrating matchups for some of the NFL’s most prolific offenses. Just peek at Caleb Williams’s Week 9 box score against the Bucs: 22-for-37 with 2 touchdowns, 4 interceptions, and a cool 61.5 passer rating.

Petzing and Goff, however, diagnosed Bowles’ tendencies and stressed them. The key to it all: Jahmyr Gibbs. I don’t need to tell anyone reading this how spectacular Gibbs is with the football. But the best part of his game this weekend was how he impacted the defense without the ball.

The first two plays below are the exact same concept. Starting in shotgun with Gibbs to Goff’s right, the running back is sent in motion to the short side of the field toward an in-line tight end (Brock Wright) and Amon-Ra St. Brown outside the numbers. The cool part of the design is in the details.

Watch how Gibbs ’ wheel/fade route is run. Notably, Gibbs angles his route very wide toward the sideline hash marks, rather than pressing vertical quickly. The key here is that it forces the cover-3 cornerback to keep his drop wide, opening space for the tight end seam route.

The other key here is utilizing Jameson Williams on the field-side slot and Isaac TeSlaa outside the numbers. The passing strength of the offense, pre-motion, is to the top field-side of the screen with three eligible receivers. TeSlaa, Williams, and Gibbs. With the motion, the passing strength changes, moving the trips side to the short side. The middle single-high safety now has a choice: stay on the field-side hash to protect against Jameson Williams in the slot vertical, or lean to the now trips side with the Gibbs motion.

Good luck. Either way, he’s wrong.

On the second time below, Petzing calls the same play, but the defense tries to correct.

Notice how the cover-3 short-side corner cheats inside for the tight end vertical, but at the last second tries to shift back toward Gibbs. Goff recognizes this correction and checks down to the safety valve of St. Brown, who sides in the flat for a positive play.

Same idea, different look

Looking back at the opening series of the game, Petzing clearly had this intent of putting Gibbs in motion to stress the vertical seams in the Bucs’ zone coverage.

This time, Petzing causes the same stress using the same concept of motioning Gibbs out of the backfield, but this time from a shotgun two-back look (although the second back is actually a tight end, who runs the delayed hook route into the cleared-out zone).

But again, notice how wide Gibbs’ route is run, ultimately fading to the outside hashes. The details create the space just as much as the threat of his athleticism. Further, notice that on all three of these plays, Gibbs’ route and the tight end’s route are all run with similar depth and pacing despite having different speeds. The coverage is stressed with precision timing.

Details are the difference between good offensive coordinators and great ones. There are many coaches that can draw up a great scheme on the chalkboard Monday-Saturday. But translating speed and space from the chalkboard to the field requires precision details with a championship-level mindset.

Influencing the linebackers

Lastly, a different pre-snap motion, but with the same focus of influencing defenders to open up space. This time, the goal is to influence the linebackers and create space in the zone for Amon-Ra St. Brown. Notice how quickly Alex Anzalone reacts to the motion to get horizontal from the field-side linebacker position. St. Brown is able to swiftly find and sit in the opening created for an easy pitch-and-catch.

It’s a short week with the Bears coming in on Thursday for the big Thanksgiving showdown. But even with less practice time to prepare, I expect Petzing will have his wrinkle of the week, targeting what Dan, Drew, Jared, and the rest of the offensive staff diagnose as the weakness and tendency of the Bears’ defense.

Embrace the fight. Appreciate the opportunity. Keep the edge.

lions.headline: Lions vs. Bucs Song of the Game: “Showdown” by ELO
lions.body:
DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 22: Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions drops back to pass in the first quarter against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Ford Field on November 22, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images

For this week’s Song of the Game, there will not be much talk about the actual Detroit Lions’ win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. It was a big win. It was an impressive performance. But it’s a short week, and a big one awaits on Thanksgiving.

Lions vs. Buccaneers Song of the Game:
“Showdown” by Electric Lights Orchestra

She cried to the southern wind
About a love that was sure to end
Every dream in her heart was gone
Headin’ for a Showdown

Despite a big win in Munich, Germany, Detroit Lions fans weren’t exactly in a celebratory mood heading into Week 11. Aidan Hutchinson had gone down—Detroit’s second massive defensive loss in three weeks—and with the trade deadline expired, there were no reinforcements coming to save the defensive line. With the Vikings seemingly on the rise with Kirk Cousins acquired and the Bears riding high off the Jeffery Simmons trade, Detroit seemed to be playing third-fiddle in their own division, despite holding the top spot. Another season of opportunity lost to injuries.

It’s unreal, the suffering
There’s gonna be a Showdown

But midweek, Dan Campbell shook the fanbase straight. Yeah, the injuries suck. Yes, you can’t replace Hutchinson or Jack Campbell. But what good is bitching about it? There are games to be played. We owe it to those who can’t help the team anymore to carry the torch.

And the Buccaneers were not a team to bring a half-assed effort. Detroit needed to turn the page, put the jetlag behind, and get ready for a showdown.

In Year 6 under Dan Campbell, the Lions are well-trained in adversity. The Bucs never stood a chance.

But Sunday’s game will be just a footnote of the Lions’ season, and with a short week ahead, the page must be turned promptly yet again. Another showdown awaits.

Bad dreamer, what’s your name?
Looks like we’re ridin’ on the same train

This offseason, Ben Johnson was already being hailed as one of the league’s best coaches in the NFL. An NFC North title and an unexpected Divisional Round run in Year 1 will do that.

But it feels like those accolades quickly got to Johnson’s head. He immediately declared that winning wasn’t enough for 2026. He dreamed of sporting the highest-scoring offense of all time. After convincing the already-convinced with a 59-point Week 1, Johnson and the Bears fell back to reality and have only scored four touchdowns in a game twice since. For the season, they rank a modest 10th in DVOA, eighth in points per game, and 10th in EPA/play—not really that far off from last year’s numbers, albeit with three games of backup quarterback play.

Meanwhile, the Lions offense has not been missing Johnson. Detroit’s offense ranks higher in points per game (28.8 vs. 26.2), yards per play (6.0 vs. 5.4), EPA/play (0.120 vs. 0.034), success rate (49.2% vs. 46.8%), and DVOA (14.8% vs. 4.8%). Ben, who?

But I don’t mean to diminish the opponent. The Lions are 8-2. The Bears are 8-2. The Lions are on a six-game winning streak. The Bears have won five in a row. Both fanbases are living in the golden times after dwelling in the basement of the NFC North for the better part of two decades.

From 2012 to 2025, either the Bears or the Lions finished last in the division in 13 out of 14 years. Now, the two will jockey for the NFC North for the foreseeable future. Thursday is going to be a a great one.

Looks as though there’ll be more pain
There’s gonna be a Showdown

If you want to relive previous Lions seasons, you can find the playlists we curated below: 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022. And if you want to read previous versions of our Song of the Game columns, you can find those here.

lions.headline: Detroit Lions stock report: 18 risers, 8 fallers against the Buccaneers
lions.body:
DETROIT, MI - NOVEMBER 22: Tampa Bay Buccaneers linebacker Yaya Diaby (0) fights through a block by Detroit Lions offensive tackle Penei Sewell (58) during a play during a regular season NFL football game between the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and the Detroit Lions on November 22, 2026 at Ford Field in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Scott W. Grau/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images

On Sunday, the Detroit Lions continued their supremacy over their non-divisional rival, the Buccaneers, as Dan Campbell’s teams improved to 4-1 against Todd Bowles’ seafaring squad since 2023. Campbell’s crew looked exceptionally well-prepared and executed at a high level against a physical team that was coming off a bye week, despite the Lions themselves forgoing a bye week immediately following their trip to Germany.

The Lions had plenty of solid individual performances on both sides of the ball, with a number of players starting to stack days, en route to a six-game winning streak. Naturally, with so many positive performances, we’ve got another stock-up-heavy edition of the stock report in Week 11.

Stock up: Jared Goff, QB

It might not have been his most mind-blowing box score for MVP voters, but it might have been his best performance of the season, which is saying something. Goff endured the relentless, well-coached Tampa Bay Buccaneers defense and came out on top. Even accounting for the absence of Antoine Winfield Jr. and the in-game injury to cornerback Jacob Parrish, it was an impressive performance against one of the best defensive units in football. Goff registered his second-best passer rating of the season (126.9) and a season-high adjusted net yards per attempt (10.9), the ninth-best mark of his Lions career.

Aside from the 47-yard seam ball to Sam LaPorta on the opening drive, the Lions’ offense started slowly, but Goff helped get things going and get the defense reeling. From the second quarter on, Goff was 17-of-21 passing (81.0%) for 205 passing yards (9.8 YPA) and two passing touchdowns. He helped open up the run game by chunking the Buccaneers downfield, picking on coverage defenders down the spine of the defense and putting them in a bind. On passes of 10-plus air yards, Goff went 7-of-11 (63.6%) for 196 passing yards (17.8 YPA) and two passing touchdowns, with his +1.099 EPA/dropback being the second-best mark against the Buccaneers’ defense on such passes this season.

Goff also played notably well under pressure, going 7-of-11 passing (63.6%) for 121 passing yards (11.0 YPA) and two passing touchdowns, with his +0.492 EPA/dropback being the best mark of any quarterback under pressure against the Buccaneers’ defense this season.

Goff was supremely comfortable navigating the pocket against the Buccaneers’ fierce defensive front, avoiding mistakes, taking only one sack, and dispersing the ball to all of his playmakers. He even bolted for a big 10-yard rush on third-and-long scramble and executed a handful of successful quarterback sneaks, contributing to the Lions’ improved short-yardage performance. The Lions are an overwhelmingly dangerous offensive attack when Goff is this dialed in.

Stock up: Penei Sewell, LT

Now half a season into being entrenched at left tackle, Sewell has been so dominant that it’s reached the point where some of the loftiest draft projections and comparisons to Jonathan Ogden, Orlando Pace, and Trent Williams have become reality.

Sewell continually displays powerful fluidity as a run blocker, with exceptional balance and secondary reaction skills. Against the Buccaneers, he was single-blocking both defensive ends and defensive tackles, kicking out defenders and even erasing defenders on the backside to create cutback lanes. On the day, Jahmyr Gibbs recorded nine rushes for 63 rushing yards (7.0 yards per carry) when running to the left side through either the C-gap or D-gap (5- or 7-hole), running off Sewell’s blocks.

In pass protection, Goff didn’t have to worry about edge rushers winning around the outside on his blind side. Across 16 combined pass protection reps against Yaya Diaby, Calijah Kancey, and Al-Quadin Muhammad, Sewell allowed zero pressures. Sewell also moved Muhammad around with relative ease in the run game.

Sewell’s well-rounded, elite attributes are worth highlighting at every opportunity because of how much he elevates the ceiling of the entire offense, and Week 11 was another unbelievable performance from him.

Stock up: Chuck Clark, S

At no point after the Lions signed Chuck Clark, following his stints in New York and Pittsburgh, and especially after his first month of the season, did I expect to see the version of Clark that made him a dependable difference-maker for the Baltimore Ravens, albeit a step slower these days.

Even with Kerby Joseph settling back into the rotation for 46 snaps (66.7%), the Lions’ newly named defensive captain and recent recipient of the green dot—the only non-linebacker in the NFL wearing one—played all 69 defensive snaps against the Buccaneers in a run-first matchup that meshed well with his skill set. Clark’s backend versatility, high-level football intelligence and instincts, effective communication, and, most importantly, physicality when taking on blockers and sound, reliable tackling, have made him a dependable player amidst the Lions’ recent defensive rejuvenation.

Against the Buccaneers, Clark was particularly effective firing downhill from the third level on early downs to fill the hole and stop Bucky Irving and Kenneth Gainwell in their tracks. He also recorded an emphatic unblocked sack up the middle to shut down a drive on third down and registered a disruptive pass breakup on a slant to rookie Ted Hurst.

Clark keeps checking boxes as he gets more comfortable in the Lions’ defense and is now the only defensive back in the NFL this season with at least two interceptions, two forced fumbles, and two sacks.

Stock down: Derrick Barnes, LB

Overall, the work-in-progress linebacker corps is still settling into its roles, but a number of Barnes’ counterparts stepped up to make clutch plays against the Buccaneers’ offense.

For much of the afternoon, Barnes resembled AOL Instant Messenger struggling to establish a connection. Barnes played 55 of the 69 defensive snaps, tied with Malcolm Rodriguez for the most among Lions linebackers, but he’s clearly no longer in quite the same every-down role he’s occupied at times. The team is still figuring out his role without his best friend Alex Anzalone on the Lions’ sideline and with Jack Campbell dealing with his serious neck injury.

Barnes was either slow to process or out of position on some run plays, and when he did click and close rapidly, he struggled to wrap up ball carriers (three missed tackles). In coverage, he was beaten by tight end Cade Otton on a slant in one-on-one coverage for a third-down conversion that kept a drive alive, while also allowing catches to both Bucky Irving and Kenneth Gainwell.

He did, however, have a nice takedown of Mayfield on a scramble while operating as a QB spy to get the defense off the field on third down, as well as an athletic and instinctive chase-down of Gainwell for a minimal gain on an outside run. The hope is that he and Kelvin Sheppard can continue working to find a role in this defense in which Barnes is comfortable and can maximize his skill set.

Quick Hitters

Stock Up

Jameson Williams, WR: A big, playmaking day for the playmaker that NFL Network analyst Brian Baldinger aptly dubbed the Motown Comet. Williams hauled in a 57-yard touchdown bomb, totaling 93 receiving yards on four catches, including a well-rounded in-route over the middle early on and an outstanding toe-tap grab along the sideline on a deep comeback to start the second quarter. He also continued to selflessly work his butt off as a run blocker.

Jahmyr Gibbs, RB: His vision and toughness propelled him to the best performance by any running back against the Buccaneers’ constricting defense this season, to the tune of 27 touches for 118 yards from scrimmage and two rushing touchdowns. Finding daylight on his clutch 26-yard fourth-quarter dash defied the laws of physics.

Sam LaPorta, Brock Wright, Tyler Conklin, TE: Arguably the most productive day of the season for the tight end room, as they combined for an explosive six catches for 122 receiving yards, while the offense relied on personnel groupings featuring extra tight ends on 69% of plays in Week 11. LaPorta’s extra effort in driving his defender into the end zone on Gibbs’ second rushing touchdown was worth a hefty attaboy and a pat on the back.

DJ Wonnum, DE: One of his best performances as a Lion, as he was a valuable member of the wrecking crew in run defense, registering three run stops while also generating three quarterback pressures.

Tyler Lacy, DL: He’s a sledgehammer in the run game. I thought he was a big part of the team’s first-half run defense efforts, while also generating a pressure on the first dropback of the game.

Tyleik Williams, NT: Like Lacy, Williams was instrumental in clogging up the Buccaneers’ rushing attack early in the game.

K.J. Britt, LB: Got the start in his revenge game against his former team and showed on numerous plays why he’s a human cinder block, including the colossal fourth-down run stuff in the red zone early in the game.

Trevor Nowaske, LB: One of the finest plays of the game was Nowaske swarming as the QB spy and drowning Baker Mayfield out at sea as he tried to extend a passing play in the fourth quarter. Nowaske continues to exemplify quiet competence at Sam linebacker.

Roger McCreary, CB: Up until the final 30 meaningless seconds of the game, McCreary had been targeted only once, and it was a pass intended for Ted Hurst that he broke up. He was largely lockdown while playing almost exclusively at outside cornerback (a season-high 52 snaps). He also closed well from the backside to stuff a Bucky Irving run.

Brian Branch, DB: The return of Kerby Joseph led to a number of three-safety looks, with Branch shifting more into a nickelback role. He played 41 snaps in the slot, more than he had all season combined entering the game and his most since the Divisional Round playoff game against the Commanders in 2024. Branch was still making plays all over the field, registering multiple run stops against Bucky Irving, shutting down a screen to Chris Godwin, and recording a pass breakup in man coverage against Emeka Egbuka.

Drew Petzing and Kelvin Sheppard, Coordinators: Both coordinators have consistently put together excellent game plans over the last month and a half, with their respective units continuing to find their identities and build momentum.

Detroit Lions Front Office, Pro Player Personnel: A lot of Twitter warriors and radio caller renegades will take unnecessary jabs at Brad Holmes for the one-year rentals and bargain-bin scrap signings, but the Lions won this game in large part because of the contributions of several cost-effective, well-scouted acquisitions in guys like Wonnum, Britt, McCreary, and Clark.

Stock Down

Fans booing Alex Anzalone: I almost feel nuts calling this out, but what are we doing here? This is a five-time captain and a Day 1 Dan Campbell guy who helped personify the resilient identity of teams that brought Lions fans more success than they’d seen in decades and, by all accounts, wanted to return to Detroit. This is the same guy who, just a few weeks ago, following a dominant two-interception performance, was more concerned with getting ahold of Derrick Barnes after the game to find out about Jack Campbell. If the consternation stems from a few questionable social media posts, get over it. He meant so much more to this fan base and city than that. I get that he’s now on the other sideline, but he’s not the enemy. Alex Anzalone will always be a Detroit Lion.

Isaac TeSlaa, WR: For a guy battling to carve out a role in this passing attack and build trust with Goff, he needs to come down with one or two of those targets.

Juice Scruggs, C: This was always going to be a daunting test for Scruggs, and while he anchored pretty well when matched up against Vita Vea in pass protection, the physicality of Vea, A’Shawn Robinson, and Josiah Trotter got to him in the run game, as he was pushed around a bit.

Alim McNeill, DT: It was McNeill’s first game without Hutchinson and his first forgettable performance of the season. On a day when the Lions’ pass rush was largely lacking, McNeill found himself matched up more frequently against the center as a pass rusher and was routinely stalemated by Graham Barton.

Skyler Gill-Howard, DT: The Lions need him to fight through that rookie wall and provide some juice as an interior pass rusher.

Malcolm Rodriguez, LB: He had some nice moments in coverage that will fly under the radar, but Rodriguez can’t be committing multiple special teams penalties. He also lost a foot race to a hobbled Mayfield on one scramble.

Christian Izien, S: Played only two defensive snaps in his revenge game and was beaten in coverage on one of them by Bucky Irving for a gain of 15-plus yards.

lions.headline: Detroit Lions’ playoff, NFC North odds skyrocket after decisive win over Buccaneers
lions.body:
DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 22: Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions reacts and celebrates after a first down against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers during the first quarter at Ford Field on November 22, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The Detroit Lions picked up a big win on Sunday, pushing their overall record to 8-2 with an impressive 6-1 mark in conference games. They remain atop the NFC North, tied with the Chicago Bears but holding the tiebreaker thanks to an undefeated mark in divisional games. Thursday’s Thanksgiving game between the Bears and Lions will have huge implications for both the North and the conference, but for now, let’s look at how the Lions’ playoff odds have changed after their 31-21 win over the Buccaneers.

Postseason odds:

NYT simulator: 86% (up 7%)
RBSDM: 85% (up 7%)
DVOA: 89.6% (up 11.9%)
ESPN (FPI): 96% (up 7%)

Detroit is about as close to a shoo-in for the playoffs as you can be in Week 12. It would take a pretty epic collapse to miss the postseason, but it certainly isn’t completely out of the question. Detroit has a very difficult schedule in its seven remaining games, including two against the Bears, road division games against the Vikings and Packers, and a tricky game against the Giants.

NFC North title odds

NYT simulator: 29% (up 5%) — Behind Bears, Vikings
RBSDM: 33% (up 7%) — Behind Bears
DVOA: 37.3% (up 17.9%)  — best odds in division
ESPN (FPI): 50% (up 17%) — best odds in division

There’s still a ton of variance between models, but the Lions clearly made some strides in the NFC North race on Sunday with their win and the Vikings’ loss to the 49ers. Interestingly, the NYT still has the Vikings with better odds to win the NFC North than the Lions, but Detroit has jumped ahead in the other three models.

Obviously, this Thursday’s game between the Lions and Bears will shake things up considerably, but it’s worth pointing out that right now, FanDuel Sportsbook has the Bears as the slight favorite (+155) over the Lions (+175).

NFC’s No. 1 seed

NYT simulator: 8% (down 2%)
RBSDM: 12% (no change)
DVOA: 10.2% (up 3.3%)
ESPN: 11% (up 2%)

Not much change in their first-round bye odds, as the 49ers look like they’re going to be very difficult to catch after walloping the Vikings Sunday night. San Francisco still has games against the Seahawks, Giants, Rams, and Chiefs, so it’s possible they’ll slip. But Detroit will likely have to play near-perfect ball the rest of the way to catch them.

Super Bowl appearance odds

ESPN (FPI): 12.9% (up 2.5%)
DVOA: 10.4% (up 4.5%)

The Lions took a big jump in DVOA this week, as the dataset is starting to come around on Detroit. They now slipped into the top-10 overall after spending most of the season right around the middle of the pack. ESPN remains even higher on Detroit, giving them the second-best odds to be the NFC representative in the Super Bowl, behind the heavy-favorite 49ers (48.7%).

lions.headline: Detroit Lions scouting report: Chicago Bears bring massive test for Detroit’s defense
lions.body:
CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 22: Head coach Ben Johnson of the Chicago Bears talks with Caleb Williams #18 against the New England Patriots during the second quarter of the game at Soldier Field on October 22, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images

It’s the season finale of the Detroit Lions’ mini “three-game season,” created by head coach Dan Campbell. It started with the trip to Germany against the New England Patriots, then back home against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, and now it’s on Thanksgiving against the Chicago Bears. After this week, Detroit gets a mini bye before starting their final stretch of the regular season.

Chicago is currently a step behind Detroit, as only other teams in the NFC North have beaten the Bears this season. Chicago’s offense averages 26.2 points per game, but in divisional games, they can’t even seem to hit double digits.

Let’s take a deep look at the Bears and how their 2026 season has been so far.

Chicago Bears

2026 season thus far (8-2)

Week 1: Defeated Carolina Panthers 59-37
Week 2: Lost to Minnesota Vikings 9-3
Week 3: Defeated Philadelphia Eagles 27-7
Week 4: Defeated New York Jets 23-12
Week 5: Lost to Green Bay Packers 31-7
Week 6: Defeated Atlanta Falcons 31-23
Week 7: Defeated New England Patriots 30-24
Week 8: Defeated Seattle Seahawks 34-17
Week 9: Defeated Tampa Bay Buccaneers 27-27
Week 10: BYE
Week 11: Defeated the New Orleans Saints 21-13

Offensive stats:

Chicago’s passing game this season has had some ebb and flow, as starting quarterback Caleb Williams missed three games due to injury, but the team survived without him, going 2-1 with Case Keenum and Tyson Bagent taking the reins. When Williams has played this season, he’s made some crazy good and crazy bad plays. He’s averaging 246.7 yards per game and has thrown 10 touchdowns and six interceptions. He’s clearly their franchise guy, and while he has his ups and downs, he’s still an impressive player and their best option under head coach Ben Johnson. His ability to extend plays is like no other, and he’s certainly a problem for opposing defenses.

Former Lions running back D’Andre Swift has been having a career resurgence in Chicago. He had his best season last year, and this year he’s looking to beat it, rushing for 627 yards, 3.7 yards per carry, and finding the end zone 10 times, a career high. The numbers aren’t eye-popping, but he’s getting the job done when needed. His backup, Kyle Monangai, has missed five games this season, but he has been explosive, rushing for 342 yards and three touchdowns. The good news for Swift is Monangai is back, so he doesn’t have to carry all the weight anymore.

We’ve seen a shift in the receiving dynamic this season, as the Bears traded away wide receiver DJ Moore. That meant second-year wide receiver Luther Burden had to step up, and he’s become Chicago’s top option, leading the team in every receiving category with 51 catches for 654 yards and four touchdowns. Rome Odunze has been steady as the number two option, with 36 catches for 573 yards and a touchdown. Second-year tight end Colston Loveland has been shoved into the starting role and has done well with 40 catches for 392 yards and three touchdowns.

The Bears offensive line has been stout, allowing 22 sacks so far this season and ranking 11th in pass-blocking (69 grade) according to PFF. Their run blocking has been their strong suit, ranked third with a 79.4 grade. An unexpected early retirement got Chicago at center in Drew Dalman in March, but the team has adjusted well to the loss. With Williams being the kind of player he is, you really need a strong front unit to keep the magic alive.

Defensive stats:

The Bears defensive line has been respectable, but they needed a boost, and they got one at the trade deadline in defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons. He has five sacks this season (tied for most on the team), three last week against the New Orleans Saints, as he gives the team more power on the line. EDGE Austin Booker also has five sacks, and EDGE Montez Sweat has four on the other side. The team has 32 sacks, the fourth-most in the NFL, so the pressure is getting there, just not as much as they’d like.

Meanwhile, the linebackers have gotten a boost from Devin Bush Jr., who is second on the team with 61 tackles, plus three pass deflections, two sacks, and two fumble recoveries. Fellow linebacker T.J. Edwards has been steady, though he has only 26 tackles, as his age may be slowing him down. These two help the defensive line a lot and make it tough for opposing running backs to succeed, as they’ve allowed an average of 94 rushing yards per game, seventh-best in the league.

Chicago’s secondary hasn’t been as strong as hoped, but it has some talent. Rookie safety Dillon Thieneman has been solid in his first 10 games, leading the team in tackles (64) and pass deflections (6), and has two interceptions with 1.5 sacks. The cornerback duo of Jaylon Johnson and Tyrique Stevenson have been well, with eight combined pass deflections and Johnson getting a 67-yard pick-six.

Injury notes

Key players ruled out: S Coby Bryant (IR), OT Braxton Jones (IR), TE Cole Kmet (IR)
Key players to monitor: DL Dayo Odeyingbo (IR), CB Kyler Gordon (shoulder), RB Roschon Johnson (ankle)

Chicago has battled injuries this season, and while most players are returning or have returned, they still miss a few for the rest of the season. Tight end Cole Kmet and left tackle Braxton Jones are out for the season, and after not playing a snap in the regular season, newly signed safety Coby Bryant is out for the year as well.

The good news is defensive lineman Dayo Odeyingbo is eligible to return this season and could give this defense a nice boost on the line. Cornerback Kyler Gordon missed the game last week after not practicing, and on a short week it will be rough for him to try and go on short notice. Third-string running back Roschon Johnson left Week 11 with an ankle injury and didn’t return. Like Gordon, I don’t expect him to play on Thursday.

Biggest strength: Offense

When talking about the Bears, everyone focuses on how well the offense plays. You have a playmaking quarterback in Williams, a solid one-two punch at running back, and plenty of weapons for Williams to throw to at wide receiver and tight end. Sure, it hasn’t been as stellar as 2025, but this offense is still playing solid football and winning them games. They have been held to under 23 points only three times this season, 1-2 when that happens, so when the offense can’t succeed, the team can’t overcome those woes for the most part.

caleb williams is a magician man pic.twitter.com/OVYA315V10
— wok (@wokdior) November 22, 2026

The Bears have had 36 passing plays of 20+ yards, tied for the sixth-most in the NFL. The run game has helped too, rushing for 1,424 yards, ranked third in the NFL. While the passing game has only produced 12 touchdowns, the ground game has produced 17, second in the NFL. They haven’t had many explosive plays on the ground, but they’re finding ways to score, and in the end, that’s all that matters.

Overall, the Bears are averaging 375.8 yards of offense, eighth in the NFL. On third-down conversion rates, the Bears are fifth at 45 percent, so it’s hard for them to get off the field. This offense isn’t as high-scoring as Johnson wanted before the season started, but it’s the best thing this team has.

Biggest weakness: Turnovers and penalties

Sure, every team makes mistakes, but for the Bears, a few things are doing damage. The biggest are the giveaways. Chicago has 19 giveaways this season, tied for the third-most in the league. As I mentioned earlier, Williams has had some low points this year as well, throwing six interceptions, while the two backups have thrown four. Williams is almost averaging an interception per game and is on pace to throw 11, a career-high for him.

When it’s not Williams throwing the ball to the other team, it’s him or any of the other offensive playmakers fumbling the football. The Bears are third in the NFL with nine fumbles. These turnovers usually cost teams games. But the Bears turned the ball over five times against the Bucs in Week 10 and still won.

Their other big problem is penalties, as this team is averaging seven and a half penalties a game, 11th highest in the NFL according to Team Rankings. This combo of turnovers and penalties usually hurts teams more, and so far it hasn’t bitten the Bears enough to cost them much, but if they don’t clean it up soon, it could end Chicago’s season.

Key matchup: Lions pass rush vs. Caleb Williams

While the Lions are third in the NFL in sacks entering Thanksgiving, this is one of their toughest matchups. Williams is a magician under center and can escape pressure and extend plays way beyond even among the likes of Patrick Mahomes and Josh Allen. His size helps most: at 6-foot-1 and 226 pounds, Williams isn’t an easy body to take down.

Detroit is also now without its superstar EDGE Aidan Hutchinson, but just because he’s gone doesn’t mean they don’t have the depth to make up for it. EDGE DJ Wonnum has taken over as the sack leader with seven on the year. Rookie EDGE Derrick Moore has started causing problems too, with 4.5 sacks in just the last three games, as his playing time has increased. Defensive tackle Alim McNeill has 6.5 sacks, as the interior of this offensive line will be challenged trying to contain him and second-year defensive tackle Tyliek Williams.

If the Lions front can contain Williams and force him to beat them with his arm instantly instead of scrambling out of the pocket to extend plays or run for yardage, this game can be theirs for the taking. If Williams doesn’t face much pressure, or he can escape, the Lions secondary we saw at the start of the year might return to form. Detroit has both starting safeties back in Kerby Joseph and Brian Branch, but it’s hard to cover anyone once the routes are run and it’s a free-for-all. Detroit contained Williams last season, holding him to 28 rushing yards in two games, compared with the 60+ they allowed him in 2024.

Vegas line for Sunday: Bears favored by 2.5

In addition to being some asshole, I am somehow on the board of a(n American) football organization in the midsize European town where I live. Recently the conference banned tackle football for kids under 12, and various teams threw a fit/semi-secretly organized unsanctioned tackle games between 9-11 year olds/went to the media to whine about how not being allowed to tackle ruins the sport after they got caught/sent a petition to the conference about changing the rules to allow tackle to be played again. So now the conference is doing an investigation on whether to allow tackle again for the under-12s.
The investigator interviewed me because one of our coaches signed the petition on behalf of our organization, and then asked me to write up a response from my perspective as a team board member/junior committee member/junior referee/event organizer/player parent/etc. (Despite being just some asshole, I may also be the voice of reason on this topic, at least in my local context.) The investigator also asked me to say something about concussion risk (something on which I am not an expert), mainly from my perspective as an American who has been familiar with the sport for a long time, but also because I hold a Ph.D. and this allegedly confers some kind of weight on the things I say.
The people who want kids to play tackle are firmly of the view that youth football is not dangerous, partly because people here suck at it so much more than Americans do. Please dump your favorite links about how stupid this view is, in case any of them might be useful.
Suffice it to say I feel like I have learned a lot about youth football, about refereeing football, and about how football organizations work in the past couple of years. I might write a diary about it at some point, as some of it is interesting and has changed my view on certain topics of regular interest here (e.g. when/how to suspend kids from sports).
Lest my colleagues in the let-them-get-concussed camp should find this post, suffice it to say that I have already drafted my response based on my extensive experience in many roles here, and I'm just looking to crowdsource a link or two and/or have an interesting discussion with the many well-informed folks on this board.

michigan.headline: Michigan-Alberts MOU - Link and Analysis
michigan.body:
Michigan-Alberts MOU - Link and Analysis

Here’s a link to the Memorandum of Understanding between the University of Michigan and Trev Alberts (per Thamel).
Background and disclaimers: I’m a business-litigation attorney who regularly drafts commercial contracts, litigates contract disputes, and advises other attorneys on litigation strategy and legal writing. My firm wrote the amicus brief signed by 1,700 Michigan alumni in the Harbaugh v. Big Ten dispute. I’m based in LA and not licensed in Michigan, but neither is Alberts’ attorney Tom Mars, and most rules relevant to professional-services contracts like the MOU are the same across jurisdictions. All that said, this is a message-board post by a Michigan fan based on a ten-minute read-through of the MOU with zero additional research; it is, of course, not legal advice.
Dashed-off thoughts to take or leave:
The fact that it’s called a “Memorandum of Understanding” has some bearing on the parties’ intent to the extent the contract is ambiguous in a relevant way, but the title doesn’t by itself prevent the document from being a binding contract.
On the contrary, the MOU appears on its face to be a contract. All the standard elements for contract formation are met by the MOU, as would generally be expected for any formal agreement between sophisticated parties represented by counsel. The terms are clear, and you have an offer from Michigan, acceptance by Alberts, and an exchange of “consideration” in the form of mutual promises; Alberts agrees to render various services, and Michigan agrees to pay for those services.
The good news for Michigan is that there is one sentence that is likely to be the focus of the legal dispute and may give them an out, because the contract’s own terms can limit the consequences of its formation: “Pending the completion of the Agreement this MOU shall form a binding contract between you and the University.” Michigan will point to this as their main escape hatch: the Agreement doesn’t exist yet, so this line arguably gives them an out.
Michigan can also argue that the post-MOU, pre-Agreement release of the deposition testimony, or some other belated disclosure or discovery, constitutes a material change of circumstances that contracts something Alberts said or suggested, or otherwise excuses them from needing to proceed with the deal.
That said:
Michigan should have phrased that "shall form a binding contract" line differently and should not have needed to rely on a single line that leaves Michigan’s rights implicit. The line carelessly phrases the issue as involving the contract’s existence rather than its terms, and it doesn’t say all that needed to be said to protect Michigan.
The contract should have explicitly stated that (1) the MOU is nonbinding until a final agreement is signed; (2) any hire is contingent on a complete background and reference check being completed with Michigan-approved results; and (3) until a final agreement is signed, Michigan may unilaterally decline to proceed with the hire for any reason or no reason in its sole discretion. I see the absence of these terms as a failure by the attorneys who drafted it and their in-house-counsel supervisors. That said, the line could be enough to get Michigan off the hook.
On the other hand, Alberts/Mars will also point to the detailed, specific terms and structure of the MOU, which go beyond a casual agreement-to-agree; the MOU's statement that it, rather than the future employment agreement, states the material terms of the hire ("This MOU outlines the material terms and conditions of employment between you and the University."); its suggestion that the future employment agreement will mostly contain boilerplate ("customary terms and conditions consistent with executive employment agreements of this nature"); and its unconditional statement that “This MOU, should you accept it, will be expanded and incorporated into an employment agreement."
I’m unimpressed with whichever attorneys drafted this for the University. Especially considering the surrounding circumstances, this MOU — in appearance (it's not even on letterhead and doesn't even have numbered provisions) and content — suggests to me that the process was rushed. The University needs to do a better job of hiring not just athletic directors, search firms, and football coaches, but also outside law firms. Negotiating and drafting multimillion-dollar contracts is not the place to cut corners.
Bottom line: All legal analysis is only a prediction about how a dispute would ultimately be resolved by a judge, jury, or other decisionmaker. This won't get that far because it will probably be resolved through informal negotiations and a settlement. I expect that Alberts and Mars will use the ambiguities described above as leverage to extract a buyout that is far less than what is stated on the face of the MOU, but is still at least in the seven figures and more than the $0 Michigan should have to pay.
