michigan.headline: 3 takeaways from Michigan’s demoralizing loss to Creighton
michigan.body:
LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - NOVEMBER 24: BJ Davis #24 of the Creighton Bluejays drives to the basket against the Michigan Wolverines during the first half during the Players Era 16 bracket of The 2026 Players Era Men's Championship at T-Mobile Arena on November 24, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Katelyn Mulcahy/Players Era/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The Michigan Wolverines got off to a rough start in the Players Era 16; in front of a sparse crowd in Las Vegas, the Wolverines got destroyed, falling to Creighton, 99-73.

Creighton is the fourth Big East team Michigan plays this season: UConn was picked to finish first in the conference preseason poll, Villanova and Marquette were picked to finish third and fourth, respectively, and Creighton was picked to finish second. In the Bluejays’ first season post-Greg McDermott era, Creighton beat a good Iowa team a little over a week ago, but they also lost to a Kansas State team ranked 106th in KenPom.

A year ago, Michigan thrived in this event, with three victories by a combined margin of 110 points sparking the national championship run. The basketball team we saw today looked like a far cry from that historically-good squad; Creighton kept making threes and broke down a lethargic Michigan defense.

The Wolverines find themselves at 3-3, losing two games in a row for the first time since falling to No. 13 Maryland and No. 8 Michigan State in March of 2025. Michigan’s roster has completely changed since then, but the turnover problems that plagued the first year of the Dusty May era have reared their ugly heads again. The Wolverines turned the ball over a season-high 17 times, as Creighton scored on the other end with relative ease.

This was a horrendous start to Feast Week for the Wolverines; it’s time for the more experienced players on this team to step up to make sure this two-game losing skid doesn’t turn into a streak.

Here are some takeaways from the loss.

Turnover troubles put Michigan in a big hole

Creighton’s defense entered this game ranked third in the country in turnover percentage and sixth in steal percentage, so the Wolverines really needed to take care of the ball, especially after turning it over 15 times in the Villanova loss.

Turnovers plagued the Wolverines early in this one, with Michigan turning the ball over seven times in the first 11 minutes of the half. Those turnovers helped spark a 22-2 Creighton run that gave the Bluejays an 14-point lead.

The turnovers contributed to Michigan’s first half offensive struggles, as the Wolverines had a stretch where they missed 11 of 12 shots. That Creighton lead ballooned up to 20, as Michigan looked completely out of sorts on both ends of the floor.

The Wolverines put themselves in a really big hole in that first half, shooting just 34.3 percent from the field while losing the turnover battle, 13-3. When you combine with Michigan not containing Bluejays crashing in (13 offensive rebounds), the Wolverines would have had to shoot lights out to climb out of that hole, and they did not.

Michigan showed a bit of fight in that second half, cutting the lead to 15 a few times as J.P. Estrella led the way with 22 points. But those comeback attempts were too little, too late.

Creighton thriving from three

Creighton has been known for jacking up threes for a while, most notably when recently retired Doug McDermott was knocking down deep threes in a baggy t-shirt more than a decade ago. The Bluejays came out firing in this one, making four of their first seven jumpers from deep to take an early lead.

But Michigan kept up with threes early, with Elliot Cadeau, Trey McKenney, Ricky Liburd and J.P. Estrella each making their first attempts from deep. But Creighton jumped out to a large lead because it shot the lights out in that first half, making 12 of it’s 22 shots from beyond the arc. They got a lot of open looks, staying a step ahead of the Michigan defense with cuts and off-ball screens.

Creighton made 51.6 percent of it’s threes in the game, much more than Michigan’s 25.7 percent. Michigan stuck to drop coverage off of screens, and the Bluejays took advantage. You could see it in the body language; Michigan appeared to give up a little bit more with each Creighton three, which was embarassing to watch.

Who is going to step up to snap Michigan out of this?

Losses can snowball real fast in college basketball, especially in an multi-team event setting with mediocre attendance; confidence can start to wain, and we’re starting to see that with the Wolverines.

Michigan needs to do something to snap out of this skid, and in order for that to happen, someone has to step up. Elliot Cadeau, Trey McKenney and Roddy Gayle Jr. all won a National Championship last season; one of them has to step up and point out that performances like this are unacceptable.

The next few days will be a real test for this team; will they play lethargic yet again in consolation play, or will we see a little bit of energy and heart? The answer to that question will set the tone for the rest of Michigan’s non-conference slate.

Up Next

Michigan is slated to play on Thanksgiving Day, facing No. 17 Miami at 3:30 p.m. Don’t consume too much turkey, Michigan fans; you could watch the Wolverines if you don’t feel like having pumpkin pie with your family members.

Michigan plays on Friday, regardless of what happens on Thanksgiving. Because of the loss tonight, the Wolverines face Mississippi Valley State on Tuesday, Dec. 1, after the Players Era is over.

michigan.headline: Michigan Athletics: Where Do They Go From Here? (long)
michigan.body:
Michigan Athletics: Where Do They Go From Here? (long)

Before I get into this, I think it's important to acknowledge my bias and my perspective.
I'm a lifelong college athletics administrator.  I've worked at several Power Four institutions, including in the Big Ten.  I've spent my career in this industry, working alongside the people who make decisions, navigating the challenges of running an athletic department, and unfortunately... watching college athletics evolve into something almost unrecognizable from the industry I entered.
I've never worked at Michigan.
I've been a Michigan fan my entire life, posting on these boards long before "Athletic Director" was in my job title.  That's why you'll find me lurking around here, essentially under a burner account.  All of this will probably have to end if I'm fortunate enough to climb one more rung in the profession.  I've interviewed for and considered athletic director opportunities at the mid-major level, but the next logical step for me is probably a senior deputy position at another Power Four institution.  At that point, I've got to stop posting (I said that the last time).
So, no, I've never been an AD.  But I do have a unique perspective, and I certainly have biases to acknowledge.  I think it's important to be transparent about both.
It's also why you'll often find me pushing back when the conversation turns to Warde Manuel.
Not because I'm particularly fond of Warde.  I know him, kinda.  I know him well enough to have his phone number... but, I'd still have to identify myself in a text message for him to know who's reaching out.  I'm not his friend, I'm not a confidant, and I have absolutely no allegiance to him.  The industry is small, that's all.  Our paths have crossed several times over the years.
I push back because it's become increasingly obvious that a significant percentage of the people commenting on Warde, his decisions, and his job have very little understanding of what an athletic director actually does -- and that is frustrating to read at times.  Especially when it is something I can speak to.  By default, I happen to be closer to his seat than most people commenting on this board.  But for the record, I'm not remotely close.
I've also developed relationships with the search firms that routinely work in this space.  I've had conversations with people at Turnkey, Parker Executive Search, and CSA.  I know people at Turnkey well enough that I could pick up the phone and call Chad, Jocelyn, or Diana today.  That's always amusing when I read some of the supposed "inside information" floating around these boards.
As for Michigan, I also don't have a secret pipeline into Michigan's athletic department.  I do, however, have friends at UofM and a pretty good understanding of how this industry works.
Speaking of which, this industry is in a terrible place right now.  Like too many of my colleagues, I've dedicated my entire professional life to something that is falling apart right in front of us.  College athletics is undergoing a transformation that has left institutions scrambling to figure out what they are, what they want to be, and how they're supposed to operate.  I've reached the point where, for the first time in my career, I've seriously explored opportunities outside the industry.
THE PROBLEM
I've said this before, and I'll say it again: I wasn't surprised when Trev Alberts was named Michigan's athletic director, but I was disappointed.
Full disclosure: I don't think he's a particularly good athletic director.  My opinion.
When Warde was hired, I considered him a B-level AD.  In fact, I wrote that on this site (when everyone was talking about Joe Parker and Jeff Long).  But the industry has changed dramatically since then, and I think the job has largely passed him by.  He's a bit of an old-school administrator trying to navigate an entirely new era.  I'd put him somewhere around a C today.
Trev?  I'd give him a C+.  Hence why I was never a fan.  Not a bad guy, but "This is Michigan."
He has a reputation as a below-average leader of people, and he isn't an industry leader in any particular area that I know of.  His claim to fame is firing people, not making things better.  That resonates with Michigan fans because, as fans, we're often short-sighted.  We want Whittingham fired, and Trev is the guy we think will do it.  But what's next?
I never said it publicly, but I had serious concerns that Alberts would come in, fire Whittingham, and hire someone like Brian Kelly two days later.  Such a Trev move.  My frustration with the Alberts hire wasn't necessarily that Trev was an awful candidate.  It was that Michigan had an opportunity to do so much better.
There were better options.
Jenn Cohen was mentioned, and I think she would have been a home run.  Her West Coast ties might have complicated things, but she's a strong leader, understands the business, and isn't afraid to make difficult decisions.
Rob Mullens, who was also rumored, reminds me a lot of Warde, although I think he's a better version.  Ten years ago, Mullens was an A-minus athletic director.  Today, I'd put him closer to a B or B-minus.  He's experienced, capable, and has done good work.  But he's also someone whose best years might be behind him.
And that's the thing: I don't think Michigan needs to find a better version of Warde Manuel.  Michigan needs to find an evolved version of itself.
The university has no juice right now.  No energy. No real sense of direction.  Its leadership structure feels stuck somewhere between the 1990s and 2010s, and the people making decisions don't seem to have a particularly compelling vision for what Michigan should look like in the next decade.
Michigan's lack of identity has become its identity.
As someone who has followed this university for my entire life, I think I understand how it happened.
I see three competing factions, and none of them seem particularly interested in moving in the same direction.
You have an older faction of the university desperately trying to protect the past.  These are the people who believe that what made Michigan great before is what will make Michigan great tomorrow.  Change is viewed with skepticism, and new ideas are often met with the familiar response: "That's not how we do things here."
Then you have another group that considers Michigan the destination.  They've made it... they're comfortable, they've reached the place they wanted to be, and they're good where they are.  There's little urgency to challenge the status quo, take risks, or push the institution forward.
And then you have newer leadership that doesn't necessarily understand what Michigan is, what makes it special, or why people care so deeply about it.  They may bring new ideas, but they don't always understand the institution they're trying to change.
Add Regents with their own ideas about what the university should be, athletic administrators operating within an outdated structure, and a general lack of leadership capable of bringing all those competing interests together.
It's a mess (and one with no alignment).
Michigan needs a strong hand.
But it doesn't need another bull in a china shop (e.g., Trev Alberts).  It needs someone who can command a room, establish expectations, communicate, and make difficult decisions without spending the next three years fighting every constituency in the building.
Many have heard me say, "Michigan has a habit of overcorrecting."
Growing up in the Midwest, you learn that the worst thing you can do when your car starts sliding on snow or ice is throw the wheel in the opposite direction.  You have to find the center, make the right adjustments, and regain control.
Michigan swerves, overcorrects, crashes, and does it over and over again.
A young assistant gets into trouble with a staff member and has an apparent affinity for following Instagram models and OnlyFans accounts?  The answer becomes hiring an older coach who can't remember whether the team practiced earlier that day.
That's obviously an oversimplification, but it's illustrative of a much larger problem.
Michigan swerves, fishtails.  It rarely finds the center.
And that's exactly what it needs to do now.
THE CULTURE
If there's one criticism I've had of Michigan historically, it's that the university has too many people who operate under one guiding principle:
"That's not what we've done here in the past."
It's everywhere.  It's in the university administration.  It's in athletics.  It's in the way people are hired, decisions are made, problems are addressed, and the institution responds to change.
Michigan has to modernize itself.
And I don't mean it needs to suddenly become some hip, cutting-edge operation that wants to be the first to do everything.  That's not the point.  Michigan doesn't have to be first, but it should never be last.
Michigan needs to track trends, anticipate changes, evaluate new approaches, and position itself to adapt before circumstances force its hand.
Here's a line that I think perfectly captures the problem:
Michigan does things the way it's always done things, and when it finally does change, it's never to innovate.  It's to emulate.
That's a terrible way to operate in an industry changing as quickly as college athletics.  Forever reactive.
Look at the current situation.  How does an institution with the resources, reputation, and infrastructure of Michigan repeatedly find itself dealing with personnel issues that should have been identified much earlier?
We've had assistant coach situations.  Sherrone Moore had red flags that deserved more scrutiny.  And now we're dealing with another situation that raises serious questions about the university's vetting and decision-making processes.
At some point, you have to stop asking how these things happened and start asking why the university isn't better equipped to prevent them.
How are the hiring processes structured?  Who is responsible for going beyond criminal background checks?  What are the protocols for evaluating candidates beyond traditional references?  Are people looking at the entire picture, or are they simply checking the boxes they've always checked?
And why are you so reliant on search firms?!  As a public school, you need them... but where is your own work, background research, benchmarking, etc.?  Who is doing the homework?  Who is independently evaluating candidates, identifying potential red flags, and making sure the university understands exactly who it's bringing into the building?  My opinion, they don't have enough people willing to roll their sleeves up, lock in, and do the work necessary to avoid these calamities.
I don't know the inner workings of Michigan's HR operation.  But I do know college athletics administration, and the fact that Michigan isn't leading the industry in modern hiring practices, background checks, and personnel evaluation -- after all of this... is a joke.
I suspect we'd find some of the same institutional lifers who have been comfortable operating under the same general rules for decades.  To them, modernizing means using ChatGPT to edit e-mails and create graphics for next month's benefits fair.
This isn't just a Michigan problem.  UNC, for example, has a remarkably similar issue.  There are institutions across the country filled with people who either can't or won't adapt.  Some have been there so long that they no longer recognize how much the industry around them has changed.  Others may recognize it, but don't have the interest or ability to do anything about it.
The problem is that college athletics isn't waiting for Michigan to catch up -- or even keep up.
Another example is Whittingham constantly putting his foot in his mouth.
At some point, you have to wonder who's managing the message, who's advising and coaching him, and who's providing the necessary guardrails.  If I were the athletic director, I'd be taking a very hard look at the Athletic Communications operation.  The fact that the head football coach continues to do this is a direct reflection of the people responsible for advising him.
WHO IS COACHING HIM?!
I've personally attended PR training with coaches I oversaw.  I've pulled them aside and told them what they can and cannot say and why.  I don't work in Communications, but as an executive administrator... I now do that for my AD.  Eventually it's my job to lead, not just stand by and shrug while the coach undermines everything even the average Michigan fan cares about.
And here's the thing: this isn't some extraordinary responsibility.  It's part of the job.  It's damn near 2027, we know how info travels, we know we live in a soundbite and caption society.  Someone should be anticipating the questions, preparing him for difficult conversations, identifying potential problems, and making sure the university isn't constantly playing defense.  That's what a good Communications operation does.
But a quick look at the unit raises questions.  Some of these people have been around since Lloyd was coaching.  Media has changed.  The landscape has changed.  So why is the department still so reactive?  I can't think of a single thing Whittingham has said recently that couldn't have been anticipated and addressed by a proactive Communications staff.  I'm honestly embarrassed for them.  Did they not know he has no ties to the university?
And that's the thing, the last three coaches (Hoke, Harbaugh, Moore) all had ties, you didn't need to coach them.  So you have a bunch of people who aren't even thinking about how to manage this new coach, they are just reacting to whatever he says or does.
Michigan needs a complete evaluation of its athletic department.  What is working?  What isn't?  Who is providing strategic advice?  Who understands the environment Michigan is operating in?  And who is simply doing what they've always done?
Michigan needs a vision.
The school I love is so slow to change in virtually every area of athletics that it's painful to watch.  It needs people who understand that the job has changed.
And that brings us to the next athletic director.
THE FUTURE
First, the university has to look inward.
Before it hires another athletic director, it needs to examine the structure that person is walking into.  What needs to change?  Who needs to be empowered?  Which processes are outdated?  Where are the institutional roadblocks?  And, perhaps most importantly, how does Michigan stop repeating the same mistakes?
You can't hire a new leader, drop them into the same broken structure, and expect a different outcome.
Do that, then go find a leader.  Or, because time is of the essence, do both at the same time.  Multitask.
Michigan needs to LEAD, not be bold for the sake of being bold.
They don't need a trendy name, or a hot television executive.  Certainly not someone whose biggest selling point is that they have the stones to fire a football coach, and not just someone who can deliver a great press conference or tell the Regents what they want to hear.
Michigan needs a leader in the college athletics industry.
Someone who understands where this business is going over the next five, ten, and fifteen years.  Someone who has been navigating the changes happening right now, not someone who needs three years to figure out what NIL, revenue sharing, conference realignment, and the evolving governance structure mean for an athletic department.
There has been plenty of change over the past five years, which means there have been plenty of opportunities for athletic directors around the country to show what they're capable of.  You shouldn't have to guess at this.  Who is leading college athletics TODAY?
Michigan needs to stop using Leaders and Best as a brand, and start using it as a mantra.
And there are options.
If I'm Michigan, the first call I'm making is to Jim Phillips.
Phillips has done yeoman's work keeping the ACC from completely falling apart.  I'm not sure how much longer that situation is sustainable, and I think there's a pretty obvious opportunity to give him an exit ramp back to campus.
He was excellent at Northwestern.  He understands institutional politics, has experience navigating difficult university environments, and knows how to build relationships across competing interests.  Most importantly, I think he can bridge the gap between the traditional Michigan faction that wants to protect the past and the new generation that needs to bring some vision and energy to the institution.
That's the appeal with Phillips.  He's not simply a change agent looking to tear everything down, nor is he someone who would be uncomfortable challenging the old guard.  He understands the institution side of the business, but he's spent years operating in an environment that demands a different level of strategic thinking.  Michigan needs both.
Danny White is another name I'd make say no.
I don't necessarily think he's as good as his brand suggests.  And he's not my favorite AD by any stretch.  But I do think he's a legitimate leader in today's college athletics environment.  He understands the business, has established a clear identity at Tennessee, and isn't afraid to operate in the modern era.
Michigan needs someone like that.  Vision and conviction.  Damn, how I feel about them personally.
That said, I prefer an AD with a more holistic approach, Nina King would be my 1B behind Phillips.
I think she's a fantastic athletic director.  She's nationally respected, understands the business, and is firmly in the mix among the people shaping the future of college athletics.  Like White, she's someone who would make sure Michigan isn't falling behind.  I also think she brings a more balanced approach to the job, which is something Michigan desperately needs.
Jenn Cohen is probably a long shot at this point, but I wouldn't hesitate to make the call.  She's a terrific leader and, by all accounts, a good person.  She doesn't take crap, but she also doesn't need to be mean-spirited or overcompensate to establish authority.  There's a difference between being strong and being abrasive, and Cohen understands that.  I have friends at USC who say "she's demanding, but in the best way."
Jeremiah Dickey is another name that deserves serious consideration.  He's one of the best athletic directors in the country, full stop.  I know some people will have a problem with the fact that he's at Boise State, but that's exactly the kind of thinking Michigan needs to get away from.
Stop trying to win the press conference and find a LEADER.
Hire the best person for the job.  And Dickey absolutely belongs in that conversation.  If Michigan is serious about finding the best person rather than the biggest name, it should be willing to look beyond the traditional Power Four candidate pool.
Graham Neff at Clemson is another name I'd prioritize.  There were rumors involving him earlier in this process, and I think he's a better than just a "solid candidate."  He's quieter, cerebral, thoughtful, and very much at the forefront of the conversations shaping the future of college athletics.  Graham is a strong leader with a tremendous understanding of the business.  I would be thrilled with that hire.
Travis Goff at Kansas is someone you have to call as you build out your list.  I understand that he's home at Kansas, but this is Michigan.  You make the call, have the conversation, and see what happens.  He has demonstrated that he can lead an institution through a period of change, and that's exactly the kind of experience  Michigan should be exploring.
Bryan Blair at Syracuse is a fast riser and someone I'd absolutely consider.  He's the kind of candidate Michigan should be evaluating if it wants to get ahead of the curve rather than waiting until everyone else has identified the same person.  If you're looking for someone with momentum, fresh ideas, and the potential to become one of the next leaders in this industry, Blair belongs in the conversation.
Mark Jackson at Northwestern deserves to be high on the list, too.  He's done an excellent job stabilizing that department following the Fitzgerald "scandal" and the disastrous tenure of Derrick Gragg.  Sound familiar?
He's demonstrated an ability to navigate a difficult institutional environment, restore stability, and move an athletic department forward.  Those are skills Michigan desperately needs.  He's proven, the opposite of Blair.  And while Blair represents the potential of a rising leader, Jackson represents someone who has already demonstrated an ability to manage through institutional adversity.  Northwestern and Michigan have similarities as institutions.
Keli Zinn at Rutgers is another interesting name.  She's relatively new to that position, and she's probably not going to win a press conference.  But she's a strong leader, a terrific person, and someone who has been placed in a challenging situation at Rutgers.  Michigan would represent an entirely different opportunity and challenge.  I wouldn't dismiss her simply because she doesn't have the same national profile as some of the other names.
I'd also have Beth Goetz on the list.  She's probably perfectly suited for Iowa, and I wouldn't necessarily put her at the top of my list if the primary objective is to modernize Michigan.  But she's a better athletic director than Manuel or Alberts, in my opinion, and you could certainly do a lot worse.  She's a capable administrator who would bring stability, and that has value.  I'm just not sure stability alone is what Michigan needs most right now.
Rob Mullens is fine.  I'd take him over Alberts.  But I view that as a shorter-term, more reactive solution.  Michigan needs to be thinking about the next decade, not simply finding someone who can stabilize things for the next couple of years.  That said, Mullens could potentially do the Hackett thing: come in, fix a few things, hire a coach, and move on.
There are probably a few more names worth discussing.  However, the further down the list you go, the more you've got to be open to looking at senior deputies, several of whom have previous athletic director experience and are ready for their next opportunity.  But should that opportunity be at Michigan?
These candidates aren't equal, but ultimately it is not my call and I'm not on Michigan's campus to know who would suits them best.  Some bring experience navigating major conference and institutional politics.  Others bring a more modern approach to running an athletic department.  Some have demonstrated an ability to stabilize departments in crisis, while others represent the next generation of industry leadership.
They all have different strengths, weaknesses, levels of experience, and approaches to the job.  What they have in common, though, is proven leadership.
They understand the industry.  They have vision. They know how to navigate difficult institutional environments.  And they have demonstrated an ability to lead people through significant change.
That's what Michigan needs.
THE TEAM. THE TEAM. THE TEAM.
The university has tremendous resources, an incredible alumni network, a national brand, a passionate fan base, and an athletic tradition that very few institutions can match.
There is absolutely no reason Michigan should be operating like an institution trying to figure out what it wants to be (but that's exactly what this feels like).
Again -- factions of the university have become so consumed with protecting what Michigan was that they're struggling to figure out what Michigan needs to become.  Others have reached their destination and aren't willing to work, adapt, or innovate.  And then there are the newer voices who may have fresh ideas but don't understand the institution well enough to bring people along.  Michigan can't be the Michigan of old, but it also can't simply discard everything that made it special.  It has to begin operating like a younger, more modern business without losing its identity... instead, just growing it, shaping it.
Michigan needs a president and an AD to bring all of these groups together around a common mission.
The next athletic director needs to come in with a clear vision, establish a modern structure, identify the people who can execute that vision, and create an environment where new ideas grow into industry-leading operating procedures.
Michigan needs to stop treating its history as a blueprint for its future and start treating it as a foundation to build upon.
You can respect the people who built this place, protect what makes Michigan special, and still recognize that the way you've operated for the last 20 years isn't necessarily the way you should operate for the next 20.
I'm sure there are people who will disagree with my candidate list.  That's fine.  There are arguments for -- and against every name I've mentioned.
But if Michigan hired any of them, I'd be pretty excited about the direction of the department.  And if I'm being completely honest, if any of those people get the job, I'd probably delete this account*** and start looking for a way to get myself onto their executive team.  Working with strong leaders to create new paths forward is one of the best parts of working in college athletics.
And maybe that's ultimately what this comes down to.  I've spent my entire adult life in this industry, and I've spent my entire life rooting for Michigan.  I don't pretend to know everything happening inside the university, but I know what a well-run athletic department looks like.  I know what strong leadership looks like.  And I know Michigan is capable of so much more than what we've seen.
I'd really like to see it again.
#FireWhittingham
***Maybe I don't need to delete anything, given Michigan's track record with HR and background checks, I'm not particularly worried about anyone figuring out who I am.

michigan.headline: Betting odds for Michigan Football at Ohio State
michigan.body:
ANN ARBOR, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 29: Jordan Marshall #23 of the Michigan Wolverines is tackled by Sonny Styles #0 of the Ohio State Buckeyes during the third quarter at Michigan Stadium on November 29, 2025 in Ann Arbor, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The Michigan Wolverines are 6-5; the Ohio State Buckeyes are 7-4. Neither team will be making the playoffs, and this game will be all about pride. Despite similar records, Michigan will be underdogs when they head on the road to face Ohio State.

Per FanDuel Sportsbook, Michigan is a 10.5-point underdog, with the over/under set at 38.5 points.

Michigan has won four of the last five contests against Ohio State — but lost 29-7 last year at Michigan Stadium. The last time Michigan won at Ohio State was in 2024, an improbable 13-10 win over OSU.

Michigan at least has some momentum heading into the matchup after beating UCLA 18-16 in triple overtime. Ohio State is coming off a 31-28 loss to Nebraska.

Ohio State ranks No. 17 in total offense and No. 18 in total defense, while Michigan ranks No. 132 in total offense and No. 9 in total defense. If Michigan is to win this game, it’ll mean the defense has another great performance. Statistically speaking, Ohio State is the better team, but can a motivated Michigan team pull off a road upset?

michigan.headline: Wolverines in the NFL: TE Marlin Klein catches first career TD
michigan.body:
HOUSTON, TEXAS - NOVEMBER 19: Marlin Klein #83 of the Houston Texans spikes the ball after scoring a touchdown during the third quarter of an NFL football game against the Indianapolis Colts at NRG Stadium on November 19, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images

A rookie tight end score his first career touchdown, while a punter made an incredible throw to keep a drive alive on fourth down. Here is this week’s Wolverines in the NFL recap.

Marlin Klein and Nico Collins score for Houston

Wide receiver Nico Collins put Houston ahead for good Thursday night with a 42-yard touchdown catch late in the first quarter. That play in and of itself was worth celebrating, but so was a rookie catching his first career touchdown in the NFL.

Marlin Klein caught the touchdown that finished off Indianapolis. Klein’s first NFL touchdown came from 13 yards out in the third quarter and capped Houston’s 26-3 win. He caught all four of his targets for 24 yards.

Stroud finds German TE Marlin Klein for six! @nfldeutschland

INDvsHOU on Prime
Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/fS7L7wS8O3
— NFL (@NFL) November 20, 2026

Collins finished with three catches for 58 yards, with his touchdown accounting for the longest gain by either former Wolverine.

Tommy Doman Jr. converts 4th-and-8 with his arm

Buffalo faced a 4th-and-8 from its own 34 in the first quarter against Miami on Sunday. Buffalo punter Tommy Doman Jr. took the snap and lofted a pass to a wide-open target for 30 yards. A few plays later, Doman was back on the field to hold for the 54-yard field goal his throw helped set up. That put Buffalo ahead 6-0 on its way to a 26-9 win.

Another week, another punter with a good arm. This time, it’s #Bills P Tommy Doman.  pic.twitter.com/p23E5p8Yry
— Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) November 22, 2026

Elsewhere, Kenneth Grant started on Miami’s defensive line and finished with two tackles. Josh Uche also made a solo tackle.

Dominic Zvada hits from 53 and 54 in Giants win

Dominic Zvada tied Jacksonville with a 53-yard field goal in the first quarter, then hit from a yard farther out with 11 seconds left before halftime. After missing wide left from 32, he connected from 43 in the fourth quarter. Add in two extra points, and Zvada accounted for 11 points in New York’s 23-18 win.

With Jon Runyan Jr. starting at left guard, quarterback J.J. McCarthy went 18-of-38 for 173 yards, a touchdown and no interceptions. His eight-yard touchdown pass gave the Giants a 17-6 lead in the second quarter. McCarthy also ran seven times for 33 yards, including a 22-yard gain. Jacksonville cornerback Jourdan Lewis made two tackles.

Colston Loveland finds the end zone for Chicago

Colston Loveland caught all three of his targets for 29 yards in Chicago’s 21-13 win over New Orleans. His biggest grab came midway through the second quarter, when he hauled in a 15-yard touchdown — and hurdled a guy in the process — to put the Bears ahead 16-0.

Colston Loveland hurdle and TD!

NOvsCHI on FOX/FOX One
Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/F1Ivvb3Pas
— NFL (@NFL) November 22, 2026

Linebacker Devin Bush made eight tackles for Chicago, while Cesar Ruiz started at right guard for the Saints.

Derrick Moore helps Detroit close it out

Tampa Bay had 4th-and-14 and one more chance to make it a game. With 3:23 left, edge rusher Derrick Moore got a sack on Baker Mayfield a nine-yard loss, giving Detroit the ball at the Bucs’ 34. The Lions turned that field position into the touchdown that sealed a 31-21 win. Moore finished with two tackles and half of a sack. Meanwhile, Ben Bredeson started at left guard for Tampa Bay.

Other Wolverines

Eagles 19, Steelers 16: Joe Milton III started at quarterback for Philadelphia and went 11-of-21 for 141 yards without an interception. He added seven yards on five carries. Pittsburgh wide receiver Roman Wilson caught three passes for 43 yards, including a 33-yard gain in the third quarter.

Cowboys 51, Titans 30: Edge rusher Rashan Gary made two tackles for Dallas, while tight end Luke Schoonmaker caught his only target for six yards.

49ers 35, Vikings 10: Safety Josh Metellus assisted on five tackles for Minnesota in Mexico City. Max Bredeson played 11 offensive snaps at fullback.

Broncos 38, Raiders 24: Kwity Paye started at defensive end for Las Vegas and finished with four tackles.

Panthers 35, Ravens 33: Matt Hibner started at tight end for Baltimore and caught both targets for 12 yards.

Commanders 22, Bengals 20: Defensive backs Daxton Hill and DJ Turner, and defensive tackle Kris Jenkins Jr. combined for 10 total tackles for Cincinnati on Monday Night Football. Washington’s Mike Sainristil chipped in three tackles.

Hot Boa- What? Seriously? FFS

Brian

Well, folks, Trev Alberts is not going to be the next athletic director at Michigan:
The Michigan board held a call Sunday, followed by other meetings since then, related to comments from a deposition that Alberts gave while at Nebraska. The MOU that Alberts signed with Michigan is believed to be contingent on a background check.
— Ross Dellenger (@RossDellenger) November 24, 2026

Alberts has apparently retained Tom Mars—god what I would give to never have to type the words "Tom Mars" again—and Mars is asserting that Michigan owes Alberts yet another absurd buyout. This one is supposedly 17 million dollars. Mars's assertion rests on the idea that a memorandum of understanding is a contract, something various other lawyers dismiss as absurd. Michigan is asserting that the background check is why they are not hiring him. I have no idea who's right and don't care. May as well throw another eight digit sum out the window for zero return. It is in this way we can celebrate Warde Manuel's tenure at Michigan.
I do have takes:
It's several years too late to fire Turnkey but do it now anyway
The whole point of a search firm is to insulate your athletic department from scandals, whether they're about tampering or background checks. Turnkey has failed spectacularly here, offering up an athletic director with an ongoing Title IX lawsuit in the immediate aftermath of Sherrone Moore's firing for being a walking Title IX lawsuit. They presumably then leaked this information to the press—do you think it is a coincidence Pete Thamel gets all these scoops?
Michigan paid Turnkey 100k to hire Kyle Whittingham, 250k to hire Trev Alberts, and used them to hire Manuel himself. I cannot find an article that directly states this either, but given that the university has used Turnkey for literally every other executive hire of note it seems incredibly likely that Turnkey was supposed to run a background check on Sherrone Moore; if so their "check" did not turn up publicly available information like the fact that Moore was following dozens of Insta thots.
Regents come and go and have virtually no power anyway. Michigan has endured a long period with several different presidents. The two commonalities in Michigan consistently looking like the dumbest athletic department in the country are Warde Manuel and Turnkey. Manuel already out the door. Turnkey should be next. If this doesn't get them fired, what will?
[After THE JUMP: what now]

A deposition is not real life
I was not enamored with the Alberts hire and if we want to talk about the merits of a Title IX lawsuit filed against Nebraska while he was athletic director we can certainly do that. Nebraska fans seem to be of the opinion that Alberts completely botched the situation that led to the lawsuit and that may make him unfit to be Michigan's athletic director.
Focusing on a wishy-washy statement in a deposition is silly. Alberts was undoubtedly coached by his lawyers to say nothing definitive, to provide no clear black-and-white statements. That looks bad when you get the questions Alberts was posed with but fundamentally I do not care about something Alberts said in an adversarial situation where lawyers are present and millions of dollars are on the line. That means nothing.
Actions mean things. The mere fact that Alberts is currently enmeshed in a Title IX lawsuit should have either been instantly disqualifying or not. It's not like it was a secret. To announce it and then backtrack on it when the apparent source of the backtracking is something you should have known well before you even got in a room with him is incompetent.
Hire Katie Fraumann immediately
Unless Fraumann has gotten unreasonably into Chicago-style hotdogs in the last few years it seems like she's the best bet to get through a real—ie, not Turnkey—background check. No one has said anything but "she is great and I love her" either publicly or privately; she was in the department for 20 years; she may even care about Michigan traditions. It is imperative that Michigan moves on from Kyle Whittingham this week and Fraumann, who was a lot of people's preferred choice to replace Manuel anyway, checks all the boxes.
This is all very depressing
I'm used to feeling helpless about watching sports. I currently feel helpless as my alma mater spins its wheels in a leadership void that extends to the highest reaches of the university. Michigan's last five presidents: knish guy, pathetic loser with no principles, amiable interim, guy who immediately announces he has cancer, amiable intern part two, C Cybele Raver. Raver's tenure starts with an incredible faceplant that immediately puts her under suspicion of being another Person Who Is Just In Charge Of Things For No Reason.
I don't know, man. There aren't even levers here. The board of regents generally just votes 8-0 on budgets; the private equity pushback of a year ago was a rare example of the board seeming to have anything resembling a mandate to do something. The MSU Men also earned the right to play their first game at DeMartin Stadium as a 4-seed.  Unlike the women’s tournament with 64 teams, the men’s tourney only has 48 teams, so the top 4 seeds in each region get a bye to the round of 32.  MSU hosted Marshall today after the Thundering Herd took down Bowling Green on Thursday.

After 90 scoreless minutes, the game went to overtime.  There were no goals in the extra sessions either, so the game headed to penalty kicks.  Even as the higher seeded team and the home team, Marshall outperformed Michigan State for large portions of the game, winning the shots-on-goal battle, 8-5. Each team made their 4th attempt, so Marshall led 4-3 heading to the 5th with a chance to win with another successful PK.  Sadly, Grekowicz was unable to make a save and Marshall picked up the win.

msu.headline: El Niño hits Spartans in The Weather Report
msu.body:
EAST LANSING, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 20: Dylan Raiola #8 of the Oregon Ducks celebrates his teammates second half touchdown run against the Michigan State Spartans at Spartan Stadium on November 20, 2026 in East Lansing, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Lots going on in the world of MSU sports this weekend. So, we thought let’s have some weather report fun and incorporate basketball, hockey and football all into this week’s report. Football was an ugly blood bath that we all saw coming. Hockey pulls off a split but had its own blood bath brawl in Yost. Basketball saw some solid bench action but the post is not looking good with the center position. Fellow TOC writer O helped out with this report and the basketball sun and cloud are coming from him. Without further adieu let us step into some sunshine.

Sun #1

My first sun is for the Spartan football team and coaches. They lost 45-7 you say, how could you possibly award the team a sun? This team has looked bad, and have had some very ugly games. This team has also had injuries that have superceded the last two years and those years were bad. What has changed this year is character. The team has character and fight. They are giving their best and not giving up. The number of underclassmen getting playing time, the number of athletes that are not the four stars Oregon is sending out there are all getting strong character development in Spartan grit. Fitz has the team playing. I’d be interested to see if he can get better athletes and take a good look at conditioning and what is going on with all these injuries. I know there is one more game but next year will really be the year to see what Fitz can actually potentially do.

Sun #2

Sun two brings us to the ice. MSU hockey has been off to a tough start and has been disappointing. Struggling to find their chemistry and identity with all the youth and lacking a true leader. Well, this weekend against the weasels MSU had an opportunity to perhaps turn the season in the right direction. Friday was an ugly game where the Spartans were manhandled and it all started with an early power play that had MSU behind practically from the start. Then we get to the melee. The hip check that the weasels felt very offended by. Barnhill and Vansaghi may have fought life back into this team. Even with both players suspended for game two and into the OSU series, they maybe let out frustrations of an entire team in an early season. Saturday night, an entirely different MSU team took the ice. Down defenders, Ward and Jurecki brought energy and the sticks were active Saturday. MSU out shot, out played, and out scored the number one team in the country. They looked like the team we have been waiting for. Yes, the weasels were short forwards, but MSU was down defenders. Ravensbergen looked outstanding, except when he left his post open, but still had the shut out. This might be a breath of fresh air that they needed to get into the winning column. The team is talented, now let’s continue to play like it.

Sun #3

Our basketball sun is going to Kur Teng. Teng had a career high 24 points on 8/11, and 5/8 from 3. Teng showed he can be a reliable shooter for this team. This allows the team to not rely on Scott and Jervis and sometimes Fears for all the perimeter shooting. Teng has always been smooth from three but has never been consistent or had a break out performance. Hopefully Teng can get hot and be a weapon that draws coverage which can perhaps open up some paint play if the MSU big men can handle it.

Cloud #1

Football cloud goes to the teams health. MSU was doubled in yardage, had two turnovers, were terrible on third down and I’m still giving the cloud to health. The injuries on this team need to be figured out. Injuries have haunted this team for a few years now. So, what’s going on? Is there something going on in conditioning or practices? Is it dietary? Is it really just bad luck? Conditioning coaches have changed and we still have the problem. This year though, was unbearable. The injuries were so much it had to be difficult to game plan when you don’t end up having the players you need on the field. It is nearly impossible to be competitive against an Oregon with third string players and a freshman QB.

Cloud #2

As much as the brawl helped inspire my hockey sun, that same brawl inspires my hockey cloud. Losing Barnhill and Vansaghi for one game is bad enough. The reprucussions of suspensions could be greater and have implications down the road. Having a significant penalty means the two are going to have to stay out of trouble or a worse suspension will come their way. That is a tough ask for a player like Vansaghi who is the agitator  for MSU. He is the guy that comes to the defense of his teammates and will throw a punch at anyone. To have him have to change his way of play could be a learning process. In a team that needs a bit more leadership, Vansaghi is a guy that can provide that, the chip on the shoulder, and the aggression. MSU needs him, so the suspensions will be something to keep an eye on.

Cloud #3

Our basketball cloud has been hinted at some but we can officially say it now goes to the centers. Taylor, McCulloch and Bonke had three combined field goals. They had six turnovers. None of them can be relied upon to be fed the ball in the low post and make a move to beat a defender. They are only scoring on rebounded put backs or a wide open Fears feed. To make things worse, the coaching staff didn’t even try to run any of those sort of plays. Bonke has been disappointing all season and Taylor is still developing. Regardless, the Spartans need a lot more production from the big guys in the paint. MSU typically struggles at the arc but has had some success there this season. If they can get stronger in the block and stay hot outside, they will be very difficult to beat. Hopefully, they can work out these kinks before the schedule gets even tougher in B1G play.

There we have it. As a big follower and fan of MSU hockey, I was very happy to see this team look like itself and take down number 1 at Munn. That was my favorite moment of the weekend. The lineup changes may be the key to staying hot on the ice. As always, I look forward to seeing where your clouds and suns lie in the comments. I wish you all a Happy Thanksgiving and be thankful there’s only Rutgers left on the football schedule. Go Green!

msu.headline: Instant Recap: Michigan State gets stomped by Oregon
msu.body:
Michigan State’s Derrick Simmons, left, tackles Oregon’s Da'Jaun Riggs during the first quarter on Friday, Nov. 20, 2026 in East Lansing. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

Whew, boy. That was the worst loss of the season.

It was all Oregon tonight. Michigan State’s offense struggled early, and Oregon scored halfway through the first quarter to give the Ducks a 7-0 lead behind a Brandon Smith 5-yard touchdown run.

Frederick Moore had a nice one-handed snag right before the second quarter started, but Liam Boyd would miss a 47-yard field goal for Michigan State’s first chance to put points on the board. The offense was starting to look solid behind Kayd Coffman’s play, but he would trip while running out of the pocket to turn the ball over on a 4th-and-3 from Oregon’s 28-yard line.

The defense did their best to keep the Spartans close, but their special teams did not. Chrishon McCray would muff the next punt by the Ducks to allow Oregon to take over in the redzone. The defense held tough and forced them to kick a field goal, and it made it a 10-0 game. Near the end of the first half, Dan Lanning called a fake field goal where the Ducks’ kicker was able to run it in from 15 yards out to give Oregon a 17-0 lead heading into halftime.

Once that fake field goal scored, it felt like the game was already out of reach.

Oregon opened up the second half with another touchdown run, this time from Simeon Price, to put them up 24-0.  Michigan State would respond with a touchdown of their own with a direct snap from the 1-yard line by Jaz Patterson, though it would be the only points they scored all night.

Both Brandon Smith and Simeon Price would add another touchdown run each for the Ducks, and Dylan Raiola found Dakorien Moore for a nice one-handed touchdown pass as Oregon continued to pile on the points. Oregon would go on to win 45 to 7. Michigan State moves to 3-8

Kayd Coffman completed 10 of his 19 passes for 106 yards and one interception. Jaz Patterson handled 16 carries, but only managed 26 yards. Brandon Tullis added 25 yards on eight carries. The Spartans’ leading receiver was Fredrick Moore with 31 yards on two catches.

It was a brutal loss, and one of those games where you wish it could’ve ended by the end of the third quarter, as Oregon kept putting more and more points on the scoreboard. Luckily for the Spartans, it’s not the end of the season, and they’ll finish it off with a matchup at Rutgers on Thanksgiving weekend. Let’s hope they can finish the season with a win.

Go Green!

tigers.headline: Tigers sign SS Ha-Seong Kim to a one-year deal, per report
tigers.body:
ATLANTA, GA - OCTOBER 07: Atlanta shortstop Ha-Seong Kim (7) takes batting practice prior to the start of the NLDS game 4 between the Los Angeles Dodgers and the Atlanta Braves on October 7th, 2026 at Truist Park in Atlanta, GA. (Photo by Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images

At Troy Melton’s extension press conference on Tuesday morning, Scott Harris hinted that a move to shore up their infield defense was already in the works. It didn’t take long, as Jeff Passan of ESPN reports that the Tigers are in agreement with free agent shortstop Ha-Seong Kim on a one-year deal worth $5 million. Mark Feinsand of MLB.com reports that the deal includes another million dollars in performance bonuses that can be earned.

The Tigers have been linked to the 31-year-old infielder in previous offseasons, but nothing ever emerged. Kim has dealt with a litany of injuries in recent years, leaving the memory of his strong 2023-2024 campaigns with the San Diego Padres a bit distant. Kim had labrum issues with attendant inflammation in his right shoulder, his throwing arm, in late 2024 and 2025 that really limited him. He had surgery on the shoulder after the 2024 season and missed much of the 2025 season recovering.

He signed a one-year deal with the Braves last offseason, but a tendon injury to his right middle finger after a slip and fall on ice in his native South Korea required surgery and sent him repeatedly back to the injured list through the year. He appeared in just 51 games and couldn’t swing the bat at all, hitting just .116 on the year. The injury also affected his throwing and it was just a disaster of a season all around.

Scott Harris loves a cheap bet on a player to rebound from injury, and this is another example. Those bets have been failures. The recent signing of right-hander Luis Gil is another example of a deal where the risk is low and the reward fairly high, but the odds are pretty poor of it working out as hoped. Cumulatively, they’ve flushed a lot of money down the drain this way with nothing to show for it while avoiding obvious upgrades that would’ve required a more significant investment.

Kim was a star for the Kiwoom Heroes in the KBO for a few years before coming stateside. He signed a four-year deal worth $28 million with the San Diego Padres during the 2020-2021 offseason. He started off slowly in 2021, but from 2022-2024 was a consistent 3-4 WAR sort of player with excellent defense and roughly league average production at the plate.

After so much trouble with his shoulder, it’s not at all clear the Tigers will even get the defensive portion of Kim’s former abilities here. The finger injury at least seems like something that a long period of rest would have resolved. Labrum issues in your throwing arm are a lot more serious, though at least there was no reported trouble with the shoulder during his attempts to get back into form last year.

This is a small enough deal to just dump if John Peck cleans up his defense a little more and looks more capable of playing an above average shortstop. The problem is actually being willing to cut your losses quickly, which is something Harris has struggled with. There’s at least the chance that with all this time off, Kim will finally be well beyond the shoulder problems and ready to start getting back to his old form.

It’s a small bet on that possibility, but one would hate to see Peck have a strong spring camp only to get sidelined again while the Tigers run another low cost experiment. It’s also odd to make a move like this and not insist on a club option for 2028 in case it works out. Hard to believe many teams were clamoring for a player who arguably should be getting a minor league deal with an invite to spring camp Essentially, this is just a depth move, and so how they handle that competition for playing time, and how long they stick with Kim if he can’t get it going at the plate, is the crux of the issue.

Infielder Ha-Seong Kim and the Detroit Tigers are in agreement on a one-year, $5 million contract, sources tell ESPN.
— Jeff Passan (@JeffPassan) November 24, 2026

tigers.headline: Teruaki Sato signs with Cubs, Freddy Peralta heads to Baltimore, and the Troy Melton extension is official
tigers.body:
TORONTO, ON - SEPTEMBER 14: Troy Melton #52 of the Detroit Tigers pitches during a game against the Toronto Blue Jays at Rogers Centre on September 14, 2026 in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. (Photo by Vaughn Ridley/Getty Images) | Getty Images

With the biggest of all free agents this offseason signed as Tarik Skubal agreed to a monster deal worth $450 million, the other big names are starting to come off the board in a hurry with a week left until owners lock out the players.

On Tuesday morning. longtime Hanshin Tigers star utilityman and slugger Teruaki Sato reportedly agreed to a six-year deal worth $120 million. The 2025 Nippon Professional Baseball MVP, who won the Triple Crown in 2026, joins an already potent Cubs positional group.

Not long after that deal dropped, right-hander Freddy Peralta was reported to have agree with the Baltimore Orioles on a five-year deal totaling $125 million. The former Milwaukee Brewers starter was traded to the New York Mets last offseason before his final year of team control. It went quite poorly, but after Peralta was traded to the Tampa Bay Rays at the trade deadline he was able to turn things around somewhat. While never an ace, the 30-year-old was a generally durable frontline starter for the Brewers. Even so, that’s a pretty big contract for a pitcher whose current projections look decidedly more like a fairly average mid-rotation arm.

The Cleveland Guardians also got into the mix a bit, signing longtime Royals left-hander Kris Bubic to a one-year contract worth $17.5 million. He’s been a good but oft-injured starting pitcher in Kansas City for most of his career. Since his 2023 Tommy John surgery, he’s had myriad rotator cuff and forearm issues that continue to limit his workload. Joining Cleveland’s vaunted pitching program will likely make him a bigger problem for the AL Central, but only if he finally puts the injuries behind him. That seems unlikely, but it’s a solid low risk speculative signing of the sort the Guardians prefer.

On Tuesday, the Tigers officially announced Troy Melton’s six-year extension which guarantees him $46.5 million with incentives, bonuses, and a club option that could make it a seven-year deal worth $80 million in total.

The Tigers officially announcing the Melton extension. pic.twitter.com/2YGpbMX828
— Rogelio C (@therogcast) November 24, 2026

There are still some big names out there in free agency. Top reliever Adrian Morejon, and outfielders Seiya Suzuki and Randy Arozarena are still available. As Sato plays some right field as well as third base, it will be interesting to see if the Cubs circle back to Suzuki at this point, but it seems much more likely that they’re out of the market for the 32-year-old.

Overall, free agency is moving very quickly and just about all the big names seem set on getting deals done before the lockout. Whether that signals a belief in the owners getting a salary cap in place, or whether Skubal’s massive contract and the flurry of signings means that players are trying to avoid the waiting game and uncertainly of a potentially long lockout is still anyone’s guess. With the Tigers still in need of some upgrades in the bullpen and perhaps the infield, we’ll see if Scott Harris has anything else to come, or whether at this point they think it better to let the CBA play out and see if the new payroll structure in the next CBA creates some opportunities.

tigers.headline: Tigers sign right-hander Luis Gil to a one-year deal, per report
tigers.body:
Apr 26, 2026; Houston, Texas, USA; New York Yankees starting pitcher Luis Gil (81) delivers a pitch during the second inning against the Houston Astros at Daikin Park. Mandatory Credit: Troy Taormina-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

The Detroit Tigers made another minor move on Sunday to shore up their pitching depth. Jeff Passan reports that the Tigers have signed RHP Luis Gil to a one-year deal worth $2.3 million, with a potential two million more in incentives. The deal is still pending a physical. Gil was non-tendered by the New York Yankees on Friday after a rough season on the mound for the 28-year-old veteran.

Gil’s career has already been a pretty wild ride despite his relative youth. The six-foot-three, 215 pound right-hander was initially signed as an international free agent out of the Dominican Republic as a teenager by the Minnesota Twins. In 2018, the Twins dealt him to the Yankees for outfielder Jake Cave. Gil developed into an excellent prospect in the Yankees’ system with eye-popping strikeout numbers, and eventually made his major league debut in 2021. The next season he blew out his elbow and required Tommy John surgery. He returned in 2024 and put together a strong campaign that earned him the AL Rookie of the Year award. A lat strain in 2025 and back issues in 2026 have limited him in the interim to just 84.1 innings over the last two seasons.

There are some reasons for optimism. Gil still has good velocity, sitting 95.3 mph on his fourseamer in 2026, though that’s down over a full mile per hour from his peak a few years back. He has good riding action on the pitch at the top of the zone, along with plus extension. His slider and changeup are both quality plus pitches. At his best he’s electric. He just hasn’t been able to stay on the mound long enough to get in a groove the past two years. His command has never been particularly good, and his walk rates have spiked as the injuries took their toll, but he’ll throw enough strikes to make it work if healthy.

We’ll be curious to hear what Tigers’ president of baseball operations, Scott Harris, has to say about this acquisition. There’s a very good argument that Gil would be better off as a reliever. He topped out at 98.4 mph in 2026, despite the ongoing back troubles. If he can sit 97-98 mph in short bursts he’d be pretty electric with a plus slider-changeup combination. At the same time, he can come to camp as starting depth if needed as well.

Hopefully the medicals come back clean. The Tigers have not had much success keeping their pitchers healthy at any level of the organization. That’s a leaguewide problem, but the Tigers have had it worse than many if we put the whole farm system into the equation. The club has already made changes this offseason, hiring Scott Peters as their new medical director and Jeremiah Randall as head athletic trainer and physical therapist, so there’s clearly an emphasis on trying to address the problem.

Ultimately, this is a small, low risk move of the sort Harris favors. Yet Gil has a lot of talent if his body will just cooperate and the club could come out way ahead with this signing if they can get him right.
